author: John David Parol, John Elvin Gonzales, Colline Nobleza, at Joanna Del Rosario
title: Edukasyon sa kuko ng komersyalisasyon
content:
Sa mga pamantasang dapat sana’y pugad ng mapagpalayang kamalayan, lalong sinisiil ang mga kabataang estudyante sa kasalukuyang kalagayan ng pagkakait sa sa edukasyon bilang batayang karapatan at sa halip ay garapalang inilalako bilang kalakal.

Sa kaibuturan, iisa ang bumubuhay sa krisis na ito: ang marahas na komersyalisasyon at neoliberal na reistruktura ng edukasyon. Sa walang-patumanggang pagyakap sa mga Kanluraning modelo, ganap na isinubasta ang silid-aralan sa interes ng pandaigdigang merkado.

Nababawasan ang diin sa paghubog sa mag-aaral bilang kritikal na tagasuri ng lipunan. Sa halip, unti-unti silang itinutulak upang umakma sa merkado bilang tagakonsumo at nakareserbang lakas-paggawa para sa umiiral na sistema. Ramdam ito sa patung-patong na bayarin, kakapusan sa mga pasilidad, at sa unti-unting pagliit ng mga demokratikong espasyo sa loob ng mga kampus.

Ayon sa Artikulo 14, Seksyon 5 ng ating Saligang Batas, malinaw na dapat itakda ang “pinakamataas na prayoridad sa badyet” para sa edukasyon. Ngunit sa kabila nito, patuloy namang kinakaltasan ang pondo para sa mga pampublikong pamantasan, partikular sa mga State Universities and Colleges (SUCs).

Sa panukalang ₱7.2 trilyong 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), naglaan ang Department of Budget and Management (DBM) ng ₱141.09 bilyong alokasyon para sa mga SUCs sa buong bansa.

Gayunpaman, hindi ramdam ng mayorya ang sinasabing dagdag-pondo. Ayon sa 2027 NEP, 43.46% o 49 sa 113 SUCs ang nakatakdang makatanggap ng mas mababang budget.

Sa Kamaynilaan, nangunguna sa listahan ng may pinakamalaking panukalang budget cut ang University of the Philippines (UP) System na umabot sa ₱2.95 bilyon. Kabilang din sa may malaking bawas ang Philippine Normal University (PNU) na nasa ₱394.9 milyon at ₱291.8 milyon sa Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP).

Sa UP Manila, classroom shortage ang pangunahing problema ng mga estudyante.

“Danas na danas naming mga estudyante ang kakulangan sa espasyo kung saan may mga ilang klase, online na lang dahil walang classroom. Sa course namin ay apat na baitang ang naghahati-hati sa iisang classroom. Bukod dito, nahihirapan rin kami mag-organize ng event na magpapaigting sana sa aming mga kampanya hindi lamang dahil sa burukrasya bagkus pati na rin wala talagang espasyo para pagganapan nito, sabi ni Patricia Jutie, Chairperson ng College of Public Health Student council.

Bukod sa kakulangan sa espasyo, tampok din sa ilalim ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ang usapin ng malawakang korupsyon at maanomalyang paggastos ng pamahalaan hinggil sa flood control at iba pang infrastructure projects.Isa rito ang renovation ng Rizal Hall ng College of Arts and Sciences sa UP Manila, na ipinagawa ng Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) sa St. Timothy Construction Corporation, isang kumpanyang konektado sa mag-asawang Discaya. Hindi natapos ng contractor ang naturang proyekto.

Sa ilalim ng administrasyong Marcos Jr., nananatiling malaking bahagi ng pambansang paggasta ang inilaan sa imprastraktura. Para sa 2027, itinutulak naman ng administrasyon ang ₱643.95 bilyon para sa DPWH, ₱113.05 bilyon o 21.29% na mas mataas kaysa sa 2026 GAA.

“Kung titingnan natin ang UP Manila, kasama rin sa budget nito ang Philippine General Hospital (PGH). Hindi lang siya isyu ng mga estudyante; issue siya ng mamamayan. Sino ba ang mga nakikinabang sa ating hospital? Mga mamamayan natin na nangangailangan ng mapagkalingang health care system sa bansa,” saad naman ni Kabataan Partylist UPM chairperson Querobin Acsibar.

Espasyo rin ang usapin sa Philippine Normal University (PNU) at Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP).

“Sa loob ng pamantasan, maraming isyung kinakaharap ang mga estudyante. Isa lang po dito ang kakulangan sa espasyo, hindi matapos-tapos na imprastraktura, at lahat ng ito ay lumulundo sa kakulangan sa budget sa edukasyon,” ani Adleann Biol, Vice Chairperson ng PNU USC-Central Student Council.

“Sa kasalukuyan, mahigit 100,000 na iskolar ng bayan ang hindi nakapasok sa PUP dahil sa kabaratan ng budget sa pamantasan. Dagdag dito, ang North Wing na mahigit apat na taon ng tinatry na i-build, yung aming main academic building kung saan nakakaranas ang mga estudyante ng kakulangan sa student spaces at academic organization spaces na labis na pinapanawagan ng mga kabataan noon pa man hanggang ngayon,” ani Michael Dave Bolima, Secretary General ng PUP Sentral na Konseho ng Mag-aaral.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does China Intend to Target Taiwan With New National Security Legislation?
content:
TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT officials, speaking under conditions of anonymity to the media, have warned that China may roll out national security legislation directed at Taiwan in the coming months. Such national security legislation would follow up on China’s recently passed ethnic unity law.

The law criminalizes actions aimed at disrupting a vaguely defined “national unity”. Although initial warnings were that the law was mainly aimed at Tibetans and Uyghurs, the Lai administration has framed such national security legislation as potentially a threat to Taiwan. Under such laws, after all, support for Taiwanese independence–or even just maintaining Taiwan’s current democratic freedoms and its de facto independence–could be construed as illegal and criminal under the law.

Such Taiwanese government officials have pointed to a number of laws, some of which are still in the review process, as potentially impacting Taiwan. This includes the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration, Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security, and National Defense Mobilization Law.

In particular, the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration could be used to prevent Taiwanese who have traveled to China from leaving. This already occurred in the past, however, most prominently in the case of activist Lee Ming-che, who spent over five years in Chinese jails on charges of seeking to subvert the state. Lee is thought to have been detained over exchanges with Chinese friends on Taiwan’s experiences regarding democratization. Others imprisoned, however, have been noted to include pan-Blue academics, who seem to have fallen afoul of espionage charges in spite of pro-unification viewpoints.

Measures on cybersecurity take place at a time when the Chinese government has attempted to depict Taiwan as engaged in cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. Such allegations seem to be an attempt to depict Taiwan as engaged in the same activity it routinely accuses China of being engaged in, seeing as China consistently conducts cyberattacks on Taiwan and probes key infrastructure. Importantly, such allegations could also be used to cement a casus belli to justify war.

Indeed, to this extent, the National Defense Mobilization Law has been warned as potentially intended to provide the legal grounds for wartime mobilization. Indeed, such a law might be necessary ahead of a Chinese invasion, particularly if the Chinese government intends to move Chinese society as a whole toward war footing, and mobilize all of society to conduct an invasion.

Still, at a time of highly polarized politics between the KMT and DPP, it can be expected that the KMT will probably deny that China has intentions for future national security legislation. KMT chair Cheng Li-wun has, of course, attempted to depict China as only having goodwill toward Taiwan, while depicting the DPP as, in fact, the ones who have sought to provoke China. As such claims to the media are made ahead of elections in November, they will be depicted as simply intended to drum up public fear for the sake of electioneering.

author: Danilo Arao
title: Discord
content:
Para sabihin ng gobyernong pang-gamer lang ang Discord ay napakairesponsable dahil wala itong respeto sa datos.

Hindi pinag-isipan. Walang pakialam.

Nagdesisyon ang gobyernong i-ban ang Discord dahil ginagamit diumano ng masasamang elemento. Wala pang 24 na oras, ibinalik muli ang app na ito dahil sa reklamo ng malawak na mamamayan. Humingi ng paumanhin ang ilang opisyal ng gobyerno. Ang dating na-block, naibalik na.

Tapos na ba ang isyu? Hindi. Sinasalamin kasi nito ang kawalan ng pag-iingat sa pagpapatupad ng mga polisiya. Importante ring isakonteksto ang pagdedesisyon sa limitado o wala talagang konsultasyon sa mga apektado.

Para sa mga hindi pamilyar sa Discord, ginagamit ang app na ito bilang linya ng komunikasyon sa internet. May bentahe ito para sa mga may limitadong koneksiyon dahil mababa lang ang bandwidth na nakokonsumo nito. Kahit na medyo bumabagal lalo na kung marami ang nag-uusap, nakakaya pa namang mababa ang bandwidth lalo na kung naka-off ang lahat ng kamera (at siyempre’y audio at chat lang ang pinapagana).

Akala ng mga nasa kapangyarihan, mga gamer lang ang gumagamit nito. Kung sabagay, mabilis kasi ang audio call sa mga online gamer na naglalaro kaya nakakagawa sila ng estratehiya para matalo ang kalaban. Pero kahit na sikat ito sa gaming community, hindi maikakaila ang pakinabang nito sa mga guro lalo na noong pandemya.

Sa paggawa ng Discord server, posibleng magkaroon ng “virtual classroom” lalo na para sa mga guro’t estudyanteng nagtitipid sa bandwidth. Batay sa personal na karanasan, mabilis ang uploading ng mga electronic file sa server, pati na ang posting ng mga announcement. At ang pinakaimportante, sa server mismo ginagawa ang mga video call na nagsisilbing online classes.

Hindi man kasing-high tech tulad ng Google Meet, Microsoft Teams at Zoom, libreng nagagamit ang Discord. Hindi kailangan ng paid subscription para sa unlimited na meetings at voice calls. Sa libreng account ay puwede ring magkaroon ng hanggang 100 partisipante sa isang group call kahit na limitado lang ang puwedeng mag-video streaming. Kung ikukumpara sa Zoom na hanggang 40 minuto lang ang isang online meeting, iba pa rin ang bentahe ng Discord!

Sa ganitong konteksto dapat suriin kung bakit maraming gumagamit ng Discord sa Pilipinas. Dahil 97% ng mobile users ay gumagamit ng prepaid, mahalaga ang bawat piso ng load at bawat gigabyte ng mobile data. Baka hindi ito alam ng mga nasa kapangyarihan dahil kasama sila sa mga pinagpalang may postpaid accounts na kayang magbayad ng libo-libo bawat buwan, bukod pa sa mabilis na Internet connection sa opisina at maging sa bahay.

Mahalaga ang datos sa mobile telephony dahil 98.8% ng internet users ay gumagamit ng cellphone para makakonekta. Kahit na may mga bahay namang may internet access at posibleng gamitin ang router para mabigyan ng koneksiyong wifi ang cellphone, lumalabas na 48.8% lang ito ng mga bahay sa buong Pilipinas.

Sa madaling salita, may tendensya talaga ang maraming Pilipinong magtipid ng load at bandwidth sa paggamit ng mga app lalo na sa komunikasyon. Para sabihin ng gobyernong pang-gamer lang ang Discord ay napakairesponsable dahil wala itong respeto sa datos.

Hindi pinag-isipan. Walang pakialam. Huwag nang magulat kung basta-basta na lang naglalabas ng desisyon nang walang malalim na pananaliksik.

Sino ba naman sa mga tagagobyerno ang gumagamit ng Discord samantalang may pambayad naman sila sa premium services ng iba pang app para sa komunikasyon? Handang nilang ipagbawal ang mga bagay na wala silang alam. Palibhasa, hindi sila apektado!

Tapos na ba ang isyu? Hindi. Tandaang ganitong klaseng gobyerno mayroon sa Pilipinas. Humingi man ng kapatawaran sa nangyari, hindi pa rin katanggap-tanggap ang disposisyon nila.

author: rti_admin
title: From Inheritance to Inquiry: The Courage to Question
content:
A society becomes dynamic not when everyone thinks alike, but when people possess the freedom and courage to question, debate and rethink what they have inherited. Every generation receives beliefs, customs, institutions and social practices from the past. Some enrich human life; others may perpetuate inequality simply because they have acquired the authority of tradition. The true measure of a mature society, therefore, is not how faithfully it preserves its inheritance, but how intelligently it examines it. In the Indian context, this becomes particularly important when we reflect upon caste, religion and patriarchy. These are not merely abstract concepts. They influence family life, marriage, social status, personal choices and opportunities. Yet meaningful discussion of them is often displaced by sentiment, identity politics, unquestioned authority or fear of disagreement. What India needs is not less tradition or less faith, but more reasoned discourse about their social consequences.

I. Caste, Religion and Patriarchy: Examining the Inherited Order

Caste is one of the most enduring forms of social stratification in India. It historically connects social status with birth and influences occupation, marriage, social interaction, and access to resources. B. R. Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste remains a foundational challenge to a social order in which birth becomes the basis of hierarchy. His analysis also highlighted endogamy—the practice of marrying within the group—as a mechanism through which caste boundaries are reproduced. The fundamental question is simple: Can the circumstances of one’s birth legitimately determine one’s dignity, status or opportunities? Modern India has transformed caste through constitutional equality, education, democratic politics, social mobility and affirmative action. Yet caste continues to influence matrimonial choices, political mobilisation, social networks and community identities. The challenge, therefore, is neither to deny caste nor to reduce it to a political slogan, but to understand how an inherited hierarchy adapts to modern conditions.

Religion raises a different but equally important question. Religion has provided meaning, morality, community and spiritual consolation to millions. It cannot simply be dismissed as superstition. A democratic society must protect freedom of belief. But freedom of belief must coexist with freedom of inquiry. When religious claims influence public behaviour or decisions concerning health and human welfare, they necessarily become open to discussion. The growing influence of charismatic spiritual figures and the wider “Baba culture” makes the question of authority especially relevant. Spiritual guidance may be valuable, but spiritual status should not automatically confer unquestionable authority. Patriarchy presents a third dimension of inherited social organisation. Traditional gender roles have often assigned authority, responsibility and freedom differently to men and women. Simone de Beauvoir demonstrated how social expectations can transform biological difference into unequal social possibilities. The question is not whether men or women are superior. It is whether gender should predetermine freedom, dignity, security and opportunity. Caste, religion and patriarchy frequently intersect within the family, marriage and community, where identities and expectations are transmitted across generations.

II. India’s Own Tradition of Questioning

The call for reasoned discourse should not be presented as an imported Western idea. India possesses a long and diverse intellectual tradition of questioning, argument and dissent. The Buddha challenged unquestioned authority and encouraged inquiry into suffering, conduct and knowledge. His intellectual approach placed emphasis on understanding rather than merely accepting claims on the basis of authority or tradition. The Charvaka or Lokayata tradition represents another striking strand of Indian intellectual history. Its materialist and sceptical orientation challenged metaphysical claims and questioned religious authority. Although much of what is known about Charvaka comes through its critics, its historical presence demonstrates that Indian thought included vigorous disagreement about religion, knowledge and reality. The Upanishadic dialogues similarly reveal a culture in which fundamental questions about existence and knowledge were explored through intellectual conversation.

Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: Unknown
title: Monitoring and Evaluation Committee on the Peace Process convenes again
content:
The Monitoring and Evaluation Committee, established as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, convened in Ankara on Monday for its second meeting. The meeting at the Presidential Complex was chaired by Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz.


Participants included Justice Minister Akın Gürlek, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi, Defense Minister Yaşar Güler, intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın, Secretary-General of the Presidency Hakkı Susmaz, and Secretary-General of the National Security Council Okay Memiş. The discussions reportedly focused on the current state of the process and the work of the four subcommittees.


Four subcommittees accompany the process


The Monitoring and Evaluation Committee first convened on August 24. During the approximately three-and-a-half-hour meeting, four subcommittees were established to address different aspects of the process. These are the Subcommittee on Justice and Legal Affairs, the Subcommittee on Monitoring and Assessment, the Subcommittee on Social Integration, and the Subcommittee on Disarmament and Strategic Coordination.


Speaking on Sunday ahead of today’s meeting, Yılmaz said that the committee’s task is to monitor the process. He stated that the four subcommittees are dealing with legal issues, social integration, developments on the ground, and disarmament and strategic coordination.


In parallel with the meeting of the Monitoring and Evaluation Committee, the Turkish cabinet is also convening on Monday under the chairmanship of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

author: groundxero
title: Labour department warns JNU management over non-compliance of orders, demands immediate cessation of layoffs and abuse of contract employees
content:
After over 1200 workers at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) threatened to go on strike on 28 September 2026 over alleged exploitation and labour code violations, a hearing overseen by a labour department conciliator has led to the management being warned over “legal implications” of repeated violations of binding labour agreements, and issued orders for immediate provision of safety equipment to workers, halting layoffs, constituting a Grievance Redressal Committee, and more. The strike has been called off for the time being under the assurance of the management’s future compliance.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


New Delhi, 28 September 2026:

 In the matter of an industrial dispute between the contract workers of Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, represented by the All India General Kamgar Union and the university as well as private middle-man firms through which over 1200 of the university’s employees are contracted, a hearing on 25 September 2026 overseen by labour department conciliator Vinay Rana has led to stern warnings for the university and private firm managements over non-compliance with several labour laws, as well as directions for immediate rectification.


 


As per the 25 September settlement, the AIGKU, on 11 September 2026, served a notice to the university Registrar and Vice Chancellor announcing a contract workers’ strike on 28 September 2026 in pursuance of eight demands. These demands sought the rectification of various alleged labour-code violations by employers that jeopardised workers’ safety, made their employment financially exploitative and precarious, and undermined their rights and working conditions. The eight violations enlisted were as follows:


 


Non-payment of minimum wages on account of alleged manipulation of attendance.


Non-grant of earned leave and casual leave and uncompensated work on gazetted holidays.


Non-payment of statutory bonus with arrears for three years.


Augmentation of manpower in view of increased workload.


Unfair labour practices against workers and union office bearers.


Termination of contract workers engaged in hostel housekeeping and mess work with effect from August and September 2026.


Non-issuance of wage slips, identity cards, protective equipment, second uniform to security guards and non-display of statutory notices.


Illegal deductions, unilateral punishment of security guards and non-constitution of the Grievance Redressal Committee.


 


Copies of the notice were, as per the settlement, endorsed to the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, and the Secretary, Ministry of Labour and Employment. The notice was then forwarded to the second Assistant Labour Commissioner,

named


Devendra Kumar Ram on the Labour Department website, in the office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) in Dwarka Sector 10. It was received on 24 September 2026, and the conciliation meeting overseen by Rana was held there the following day.


 


JNU is the principal employer responsible for the welfare of the aggrieved employees, but like most disputes in the contracting era, not the sole one. Two private security firms, Rakshak Securitas Pvt. Ltd. and A.E. Securitas Security and Allied Services (the security contractors of the university), along with Q Group (contractors of housekeeping staff in the university hostels) and Max Maintenance Services Pvt. Ltd. (contractors of maintenance staff) were also named.


 


Such conciliation proceedings take place in industrial disputes under Section 53 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.


 


AIGKU was represented by its President, Sucheta De, along with State Secretary of the All India Central Council of Trade Unions (AICCTU, which is a major Indian trade union affiliated with the CPI(ML) Liberation), Surya Prakash (State Secretary, AICCTU), Vice President of AIGKU’s JNU unit, Surya Prakash, and a member of AIGKU’s Executive Council, Manikant Patel.


 


JNU was represented by its Deputy Registrar and Labour Welfare Officer Abhishek Kumar Singh; Section Officer (Legal) Vineet Kumar Bizenia; “Assitant Admin (sic)” Imran Kataria; Sanitation Inspector Saurabh Kumar and Data Entry Operator Sandeep Kumar. author: Joseph Bognot at Ara Jane Credo
title: Mula Martial Law hanggang ngayon, nagpapatuloy ang laban para sa tahanan at kabuhayan
content:
Hindi lamang alaala ng nakaraan ang bitbit ng mga lumahok sa malawakang kilos-protesta noong Setyembre 21.

Para sa mga nagprotesta, ang mga aral at pakikibaka noong diktadurang Marcos Sr. ay hindi iba sa kalagayan sa ilalim naman ngayon ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. kung saan nagpapatuloy ang kalbaryo ng maralita para sa tirahan, kabuhayan at karapatan.

Kasabay ng paggunita sa ika-54 na anibersaryo ng deklarasyon ng Martial Law, inilabas ng mga maralita sa lansangan ang mga suliraning kinakaharap nila sa araw-araw partikular sa banta ng demolisyon, kawalan ng katiyakan sa tirahan, pagbaha sa mga komunidad, at patuloy na pagtaas ng presyo ng pagkain at iba pang batayang serbisyo.

Hindi na bago sa mga maralita ang pangambang mawalan ng tirahan bunsod ng mga proyektong pangkaunlaran.

Ilang araw matapos ang deklarasyon ng Martial Law noong Setyembre 1972 sa ilalim ng diktadurang Marcos Sr., nilagdaan ang Letter of Instruction No. 19 na nag-utos sa pagpapaalis ng mga itinuturing na “illegal structures” sa mga lugar gaya ng mga pampang ng ilog at kanal, riles ng tren, at iba pang pampubliko at pribadong lupain.

Sa Tondo, nagkaroon ng kaliwa’t kanang demolisyon sa mga komunidad sa Tondo Foreshore. Kabilang sa mga lugar na naapektuhan ang mga komunidad sa paligid ng Parola at iba pang bahagi ng Tondo na saklaw ng mga planong pagpapaunlad sa North Harbor at Tondo Foreshore.

Noong 1974, nilikha naman sa pamamagitan ng Presidential Decree No. 570 ang Tondo Foreshore Development Authority upang ipatupad ang mga programa sa pagpapaunlad ng lugar. Sa mga sumunod na taon, isinulong ng administrasyong Marcos Sr. ang Tondo Foreshore-Dagat-Dagatan Urban Development Project, na kinapapalooban ng pagpapaunlad ng lugar, land tenure at relokasyon ng mga residenteng maaapektuhan.

Makalipas ang mahigit limang dekada, muling humaharap ang mga maralita sa Tondo at Port Area ng pangamba sa katiyakan sa paninirahan kaugnay ng itinatayong North-South Harbor Bridge (NSHB), isang malaking proyektong pang-imprastraktura sa ilalim ng administrasyong Marcos Jr.

Para kay Julia Barquin, lider-kababaihan sa Baseco, hindi lamang pagkawala ng tahanan ang nakataya sa proyekto kundi pati ang kabuhayang matagal nang nakaugat sa kanilang komunidad.

“Mawawalan kami ng pamumuhay. Madaling maghanap ng kabuhayan sa Maynila, katulad ng pagbabalat ng bawang, pagtitinda ng mga kakanin at street food. Hindi katulad ng mga lilipatan na walang hanapbuhay, umpisa na naman,” ani Barquin.

“Kaya nandito kami ngayon at sumama sa pagkilos na ito dahil ipinapanawagan namin yung karapatan namin bilang mga naninirahan sa komunidad ng Tondo. Huwag naman kaming i-demolish bilang inyong nasasakupan at kilalanin yung karapatan namin bilang naninirahan sa komunidad,” dagdag pa niya.

Makasaysayan na rin ang pakikibaka ng mga maralita sa Tondo Foreshore laban sa demolisyon, harassment at iba pang usapin hinggil sa katiyakan sa paninirahan. Noong 1970, bago pa ideklara ang Martial Law, itinatag ng mga residente ang Samahan ng Mamamayan-Zone One Tondo (SM-ZOTO), na naglunsad ng iba’t ibang kampanya at paglaban sa banta ng demolisyon. Sa kasalukuyan, iba’t ibang samahan at grupo ng mga residente ang tumitindig kaugnay ng nagpapatuloy nilang kalbaryo sa paninirahan.

Kasabay nito, inalala ni Barquin ang sunod-sunod na sunog na tumama sa mga komunidad sa Tondo Foreshore, partikular sa Parola at Baseco, ngayong taon.

Noong Marso 6, isang sunog sa Parola ang nag-iwan ng 349 pamilyang nawalan ng tirahan. Hindi pa man nakakabangon ang komunidad mula sa trahedya, muling nilamon ng apoy ang Parola noong Mayo 23, na nakaapekto sa mahigit 7,000 indibidwal o 2,134 pamilya.

Ilang araw lamang ang lumipas, sumiklab naman ang sunog sa bahagi ng Gasangan, Baseco noong Mayo 30, na nakaapekto sa higit 85 pamilya o 340 indibidwal. Isang menor de edad ang nasawi sa insidente.

Sa gitna ng magkakasunod na sunog, isinagawa naman noong Mayo 20 ang groundbreaking ceremony para sa NSHB sa Baseco.

Sa Baseco at Parola, nakatakdang dumaan ang 2.026-kilometrong tulay na mag-uugnay sa Parola sa North Harbor at Baseco sa South Harbor. Nauna nang inaprubahan ang NSHB sa ilalim ng administrasyong Duterte at iginawad ang kontrata sa China Road and Bridge Corporation.

Ipinagpatuloy naman ito sa ilalim ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. bilang bahagi ng infrastructure flagship projects sa ilalim ng Build Better More program na nagkakahalagang P6.753 bilyon.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Did the KMT Reverse Course on Drone Spending?
content:
AFTER MUCH political contention about the budget earlier this year–including Taiwan’s defense spending–the KMT eventually relented and passed the national budget after over 200 days of stalling at the end of last month. Though the KMT had originally proposed cutting or freezing drone spending–in fact, suggesting that it might cut or freeze all budget that would have been allocated to drones, this did not come to pass.

The KMT seemed to have suddenly become aware of the poor optics of blocking drone spending after an article in The Economist, which lashed out at the KMT as obstructionist and self-interested for continuing to block drone spending when this could be vital to Taiwan’s defense against Chinese threats. In short order, then, the KMT legislative caucus suddenly had a reversal of course.

Nevertheless, the KMT’s approval of drone funding places this under the central government budget, rather than as a special budget. The original special expenditure for drone spending that the Lai administration originally hoped to pass was 210 billion NT for three specific drone systems, which would have been unmanned aerial vehicles and maritime drones.

The 240 billion NT passed by the KMT was for all military drone spending, not just those specific three systems, and annual spending would be capped at 40 billion NT. 31 billion was originally budgeted by the military for unmanned systems, while the three additional systems sought by the military would require 42.1 billion NT.

As such, the military originally intended to spend more than 70 billion NT, which means that a reduction of 30 billion NT has taken place in the version passed by the KMT. Likewise, with the KMT’s version of the bill, the 40 billion NT in annual drone spending is subject to yearly approval, which may mean perpetual uncertainty for the drone industry–which cannot count on future funding. According to experts, building up the drone industry usually requires larger initial spending, after which spending falls, rather than the mechanical application of the same amount of funding per year. As a result, the KMT’s version of drone spending ultimately will be detrimental to drone development.

Even before the public backlash that took place in the wake of The Economist article, KMT heavyweights such as Jaw Shaw-kong had warned that it would be political suicide for the KMT to continue to oppose drone spending to the hilt. In this sense, the KMT may have eventually realized the poor optics of trying to freeze or cut all drone spending whatsoever. At the same time, one notes that drone cuts could impact the KMT’s base in Taichung and other areas that have invested in the drone spending.

Anger against the KMT from pan-Green partisans over its efforts to sabotage defense is expected to continue, of course, but it is still a question as to whether this will translate to society at large. And fractures in the KMT may widen, seeing as some KMT politicians are cautious of the possible electoral backlash from the perception that the political party simply aims to undermine Taiwan’s defense.

author: Alex Salmon
title: The absent history of social upheaval after WWI
content:
Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I By Fiona Skyring Perth: UWA Press November, 2025 225pp RRP $39.99

Peace Day celebrations were held across Australia on November 14, 1918, following the end of World War I.

Even though the shooting had barely ended, the social tensions created by the war would be exposed in riots and brawls involving returned soldiers in Adelaide, Broken Hill and Townsville. These were predecessors to the riots that occurred from 1919–21.

Author and historian Fiona Skyring explores this history in her 2025 book, Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I.

In Townsville and Broken-Hill, riots and brawls occurred between self-styled “loyalist” soldiers and trade unionists, socialists and anti-conscriptionists. In Adelaide, soldiers showed their support to striking tram drivers, 300 of whom had served in the Australian Imperial Forces (AIF), by organising and attacking strikebreakers.

The Australia that WWI soldiers returned to was deeply divided by class, religion, social and political issues. The country had been rocked by the 1916–17 anti-conscription referenda, the 1917 New South Wales general strike, and international events such as 1916 Irish Easter Uprising, the 1917 Russian Revolution and the 1918–19 influenza pandemic.

In 1918–19 these divisions continued, as the country experienced a cost-of-living crisis, which was compounded by the mass bereavement due to the war.

Industrial upheaval continued in 1919 with 6.3 million days lost to industrial action, figures unmatched even in the 1970s. The largest strike was waged by the Seamen’s Union, which shut down wharves across the country between May and August.

In Riots, Skyring examines the way the ANZAC legend was being constructed by writers such as Charles Edwin Woodrow Bean, even as WWI continued.

In Bean’s ANZAC Book, published in 1916, the stories of soldiers who said they didn’t want to fight, thought their comrades’ deaths were futile and felt the class divisions between officers and ordinary soldiers in the AIF, were excluded.

Bean wrote in 1919: “Australia (has become) a new nation. Five years ago, the world barely knew her. Today, the men who went to fight for her have placed her high in the world’s regard.”

The celebrated legend of the ANZAC was dominated by the ideal of the overwhelmingly white, tough man from the bush; a classless citizen soldier whose sacrifice was made in the name of nation, empire and freedom. This narrative excluded the 1000 Aboriginal men who served in the AIF and who would experience more discrimination upon their return after the war’s end.

The message that civilian society should honour the soldiers’ sacrifice and any criticism of WWI being seen as “an attack on the soldiers” made it easy for right-wing politicians, industrialists and organisations such as the Returned Soldiers and Sailors Imperial League of Australia (RSSILA) to paint anti-war activists, trade unionists, socialists, Irish republicans and members of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) as “disloyal”.

When 1000 socialists and members of Brisbane’s Russian exile community carried red flags on a march through the city in defiance of the 1914 War Precautions Act, on March 23 1919, the conservative press and other forces in collaboration with military intelligence whipped up xenophobic anti-communist sentiment.

This resulted in a crowd of 7-8000 returned soldiers marching to South Brisbane, attacking the headquarters of the Russian Workers’ Association and engaging in an anti-Russian pogrom. These events became known as the Red Flag Riots.

Further soldier’s riots would occur in Fremantle, Melbourne, Kalgoorlie-Boulder and Sydney between 1919 and 1921. The Sydney 1921 riots inspired D H Lawrence’s 1923 book, Kangaroo.

However, the soldiers’ riots were not all directed against socialists and trade unionists.

Skyring describes the events of November 1918, when returned soldiers acted in solidarity with striking tram drivers in Adelaide by attacking strikebreakers.

Soldiers returning home on a troop ship to Fremantle Port in Western Australia on May 5, 1919, also gave their support to striking lumpers – workers who loaded and unloaded shipping cargo. There are accounts of soldiers fighting with police on Fremantle’s streets, in the days following.

In Melbourne, soldiers fought police for four days straight, in July 1919, over the lack of …

author: Danica Rachel
title: Protest called against October arms fair in Perth
content:
The Land Forces Exposition 2026, to be held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on 6-8 October, will be a three-day extravaganza of exhibitions, talks and luncheons, where the main topic of conversation is how best to kill people. More than 20,000 weapons company executives, politicians and military personnel from around the world are expected to attend.

We have to protest against this outrageous celebration of death and destruction.

Photos from the 2024 event on the front page of the

Land Forces website

 are enough to make you ill. A smiling representative of Anduril, a company specialising in AI-powered warfare, shows off a battle drone. A live demonstration of a robot dog, presumably designed to carry autonomous weapons, takes place on the exhibition floor. A drone as big as a car hangs from the ceiling.

Lockheed Martin, the world’s biggest arms dealer—and builder of the F-35 fighter jets Israel uses to bomb Gaza—will have its latest death machines on display. As will Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons company.

Senior executives from Anduril and BAE Systems will speak on a panel discussing “the realities of Ukraine, Iran and other current conflicts”. Today’s bloodshed used as a case study to make tomorrow’s killing more efficient. What could those “other conflicts” be? Israel’s invasion of Lebanon? One assumes that there’s much these monsters have learned from Gaza, too.

Lockheed Martin and BAE will be joined by Babcock, Boeing, Honeywell, Northrop Grumman and Thales. Aside from all having had significant roles in providing Israel’s weapons for use in Gaza, they are all on the exclusive list of companies involved in creating nuclear weapons.

The list goes on, and on, and on. More than 650 companies will have exhibits on the floor, all of them dealing in weapons, military hardware or AI systems for warfare.

To say the state Labor government is rolling out the red carpet for this smorgasbord of warmongers would be an understatement. It is going above and beyond to keep conference-goers comfortable by pouring $11.5 million into security.

Special legislation gives police the power to set up checkpoints, stop and search anyone for any reason, and ban anyone they like from a significant section of Perth’s CBD, including a major train and bus station, for ten days surrounding the event.

Police Minister Reece Whitby said of the laws: “We saw the scenes that occurred when Land Forces was held in Melbourne in 2024, and we do not want to see anything like that here in Perth”. Whitby was referring to the

protest by 1,500 people

 against the last iteration of this festival of death.

None of this—the war profiteering, the authoritarian police powers, the increased drive towards a world of total war—should pass without protest.

So a coalition of anti-war and Palestine solidarity organisations has called a demonstration against Land Forces on 6 October, 5pm, at Yagan Square in the Perth CBD. We need as many people as possible to make it clear that we reject Land Forces and everything it represents.

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists’ election campaign in full swing
content:
The Victorian state election will take place in just over two months, on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Socialists’ campaign is now in full swing, with local campaign activity taking place daily across Melbourne and regional Victoria.

The scale of the campaign—with VS candidates set to run in all 88 lower house seats and all eight upper house regions across Victoria—is beyond anything the socialist left in Australia has attempted for generations (if ever). Even just a few years ago, a statewide campaign like this would have been unthinkable. That it’s happening at all is something of a breakthrough.

Between 1 June and 19 September, VS volunteers knocked on more than 80,000 doors, already well on track to reach the 2022 campaign total of around 190,000. The party received around 2,000 requests for campaign signs to be put on front fences and in yards, eclipsing the 2022 total of 1,000, with hundreds of orders a week still coming in. More than 2,400 people donated to the campaign, and almost 1,800 registered for a party event. 

New branches are springing up everywhere. Wherever they do, we’re finding people who want to get involved. VS events in places like Pakenham, a suburb on the far south-eastern fringe of Melbourne—more than 50 kilometres from the CBD—are attracting many new faces. And we now have active branches in regional centres including Geelong, Warrnambool, Ballarat and Bendigo, and the beginnings of branches in Shepparton, Wodonga and Warragul. 

We’re accustomed to being almost completely overlooked by the mainstream media, but the sheer size of our campaign this time means we’re increasingly difficult to ignore.

ABC News reported

 on the VS campaign launch on 1 August, and Channel 9 reported on our “all-in” Footscray doorknock on Sunday 16 August, which was attended by more than 350 volunteers. VS candidate for the Northern Metro upper house region Omar Hassan has become something of a regular fixture on talkback radio 3AW’s morning show with Tom Elliot—most recently on the topic

“what is socialism?”

VS candidates in the regions are attracting particular attention.

Hera Sheppard,

 in the seat of

South-West Coast

 (comprising Warrnambool, Port Fairy, Portland and surrounds), has been featured in several articles in the

Warrnambool Standard

, including the front cover. An

article at ABC News

 and an appearance on ABC Radio followed—the latter

drawing the ire

 of Australia’s richest billionaire Gina Rinehart, who objected to Hera’s claim that she was pushing for Australians to work for $2 a day (in the 2012 quote Hera referenced, Rinehart worried about Australia’s competitiveness when “Africans want to work, and its workers are willing to work for less than $2 per day”). It certainly helps that, at 18, Hera is one of the youngest candidates ever to run for parliament in Australia, but regional media in general have shown a keen interest in VS candidates everywhere. 

Signs also suggest the campaign is resonating. In Footscray, where VS volunteers have already knocked on around 17,000 doors, and the campaign has put up more than 200 yard signs, a steady trickle of people have turned up to volunteer at the campaign office after receiving VS material.

There’s no escaping the fact that politics in Victoria has shifted decisively to the right, and it’s likely either a Liberal or a Liberal-One Nation Coalition government will be elected on 28 November. But there’s no shortage of people who are horrified by the rise of One Nation and who are relieved to find, when visited by a VS volunteer, that there’s a party offering a genuinely anti-establishment alternative on the left. 

Hassan tells the story of Mary, an 82-year-old he met while doorknocking in the outer northern suburb of Thomastown. A long-time Labor voter, Mary told Omar that she wouldn’t vote for the ALP this time because “they’ve completely lost their way”. He later recounted:

She described playing with all the Italian and Yugoslav kids, going to each other’s houses and having great fun. ‘It made life richer, having all the different cultures, growing up together’.

author: AWSM
title: Errico Malatesta – Vote? What For?
content:
George: This beer’s not too bad, is it?

Jack: Yes, it’s alright, but what a price!

George: Shocking – especially when you remember what things used to cost. Still, you can’t wonder with all these taxes. It costs you twice as much to live as it used to. They put up the price of some things, and say you can do without them. But you can’t do without bread, and food, and clothes – you have to pay the rent all the same, and then there are the taxes on this and the rates – on our wages too! What a life! And it’s our own fault! If we wanted to we could alter things. The working class has the remedy in its own hands.

George: Easy enough! You’ve got a vote?

Jack: What’s that got to do with it?

George: Have you, or haven’t you?

Jack: Well, I’m entitled to a vote – but I never make use of it.

George: There you are! You’ve got a vote, but you just won’t take the trouble to use it, and then you wonder why things are so bad. You deserve all you get, honestly! People like you are responsible for all the trouble in the world!

Jack: Alright, alright, keep your hair on! Just tell me what’s the good of voting?

George: It’s obvious. Who makes the laws? The M.P.’s. Elect good M.P.’s and you get good laws.

Jack: Good councillors and good M.P.’s? We’ve heard that for a long time. But you’d have to be deaf, dumb, and blind not to notice it’s the same stooges that always get in. Oh, it’s wonderful to hear them when they’re after votes at election time. They pat you on the back, ask after the wife and kids, kiss the baby, promise you railways, bridges, work, cheap bread, less taxes, higher wages, protection – absolutely everything! And once they get in, they’re no better than anyone else. Goodbye promises! The wife and kids may starve, there’s no more or less work than before, the whole town can be falling to pieces for all they care. They’ve other things to think about than your troubles! Then a few years later they start the ballyhoo again. It doesn’t matter what colour the party is: they’re all the same. As soon as they’re elected, they forget all about you. They’re in their clubs and at their select dinners, and they don’t even trouble to come and have a look at you until the next election.

George: That’s correct! But why elect the rich? Don’t you know that the rich only live on the work of the masses? So how do you expect them to worry about the masses? All they think of is getting as much out of the ordinary man as they can.

Jack: Now you’re talking! But it’s not only the rich. There’s the other type, who want to get elected so they can become rich.

George: That’s true. So don’t let’s vote for them. Let’s elect workers, experienced friends of ours, as you might say, and then we won’t be fooled.

Jack: Oh, we’ve got some of your “experienced friends” in now, and they’re no different from our acknowledged enemies! Anyhow, what do you mean, “let’s elect – let’s elect.” As if we – you and me – could do as we like!

George: But it’s not only us two. If each one of us tried to convert other people and they would do the same, labour would have a majority, and we could elect whoever we liked. And that’s when we could form a government of the workers, and then . . .

Jack: And then it would be a paradise – I mean for those who were in Parliament! You’re arranging things a bit too quickly! Those in command always have the majority. The rich are always in power. Just imagine a poor worker, perhaps with an ill wife and four hungry kids, and you tell him to risk his job and get thrown out of his house to starve; just to give his vote to a candidate his master doesn’t like. Just try and convince those poor devils who can be thrown out of work by their boss whenever he likes. They’re never free; if they want to be free, they don’t want to waste their time voting – just take what they need.

George: But if we didn’t do that, no-one would vote. We couldn’t go to the workers and ask them to vote for our party, and say at the same time that votes were useless.

Jack: That’s just it! And on top of that you have to make election promises you know you can’t keep. And then you have to stand in with the Government, and mix with the well-to-do, and all the rest of it. As soon as any of your men are elected they have to kow-tow to the people you admit are the opponents of the workers. So why the hell talk about propaganda when the first thing you do is to counteract propaganda?

George: But you must admit, it’s an advantage to have our own men with …

author: Tom Bramble
title: What’s the deal with productivity?
content:
The bosses are trying to convince workers that lower corporate taxes, fewer regulations and workers’ rights, and less union power would be good for real wages. What they really want is more profits at the expense of the working class.

For years, business lobby groups have decried what they call Australia’s “productivity crisis”. They don’t say workers are producing less than they used to; they say they aren’t increasing production as quickly as before and aren’t keeping pace with overseas productivity growth.

It’s true: growth in workers’ hourly output has slowed over the past decade, and Australian workers don’t produce as much value for the bosses as American workers. But the bosses argue that this means living standards are held back, and prices rise more than they otherwise would, contributing to the cost-of-living crisis.

They say that government regulations (rules about wages, hours of work, health and safety standards, construction standards, environmental protections and professional and occupational registration requirements) and trade unions are preventing business investment. Their solution is “deregulation”, “slashing red tape”, “more competition”. These are simply code words for attacking the working class.

Let’s break this down. First, what is productivity? The simplest definition is “output per hour”. For BlueScope Steel, it could be tonnes of steel produced per hour per worker. For a childcare centre operator, it could be the number of children in care per worker per day. Lift those and productivity rises.

But who benefits? Does the steel worker or childcare worker see their wage rise automatically if they get more done? Of course not. In the first instance, all the money made from extra production by every group of workers goes to the capitalists, not the workers. Workers’ standard of living depends on how much they fight for. And that applies across the whole economy.

The bosses say some of the additional money coming in from workers’ extra effort will come back through higher wages and maybe more jobs. They argue: “a rising tide lifts all boats”. Is that true, though?

First, productivity in Australia may have slowed in the past couple of decades, but it has still risen. Yet household living standards are no higher than they were in 2012. There is no indication that workers are seeing any of the higher value they produce in the form of higher real wages.

A starker example is the United States, which bosses always point to as the high-productivity benchmark, where output per worker is higher and rising faster. In that country, workers’ share of national income is now at its lowest since World War Two—the productivity gains have gone to the capitalists, who have grown ever wealthier at workers’ expense.

Take things down another level. Even if bosses shared a cut of the higher revenue from increased productivity with workers, or unions successfully struck to extract a higher wage, bosses would still be ripping off workers.

All wealth ultimately comes either from the world’s natural resources or from human labour. You only have to see what happens when workers go on strike to see the truth of this—nothing gets produced, not a wheel turns, the childcare centres lie empty. All the machinery, all the factories, all the railway lines can only be put to good use if workers labour on them. And these in turn are the product of previous generations of workers’ labour.

What the capitalists call productivity should really be called exploitation: the extraction of value from the worker over and above the cost of their reproduction, i.e. what is necessary to get them to come to work each day in the form of wages. They call it profit; in fact, it’s theft from the worker.

This theft lies at the heart of capitalism. It explains why the workers labour their whole lives and have not much more than their home to hand on to their kids, and often not even that. While their employer has significantly expanded their operations at the workers’ expense. Some of the bosses may blow the money on a more self-indulgent lifestyle, but personal greed doesn’t get to the heart of it.

Every boss is driven to extract more from their workers, i.e. to lift productivity, because if they don’t, their rivals will, and they will be undercut and go out of business. The winner is the boss who can exploit their workers the most. That’s why every boss in every country demands that governments make it easier for them to rip off their …

title: 10 essential new protest albums everyone needs to hear
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for September.

US rapper Macklemore called for a "free Palestine" from the stage while supporting pop megastar Ed Sheeran on September 4. His speech, along with his politically-themed set, sparked a petition from the Israeli American Council. Jewish billionaire Robert Kraft refused to let Macklemore play at a stadium he owns and rallied other stadium owners to do the same. Sheeran - who claims to be politically neutral despite supporting multiple leftist causes in the past - announced he was dropping Macklemore from the tour. As a result, all of Sheeran's support acts dropped out to protest against Macklemore's cancellation. On the same day Macklemore kicked off the controversy, US-Jordanian rapper Eddy Mack released his new album, which opens with the pro-Palestine song "Can't Cancel Me". Days later, he posted a photo of himself with Macklemore, who then announced his own "Free Palestine" tour. LISTEN>>>

World leaders walked out on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the United Nations in New York on September 24 as he defended the genocide of Palestinians. On the same US visit, he had been due to meet the world's richest person, Elon Musk, who placed a satellite in orbit for Israel last year. Meanwhile, Musk blasted a new documentary about him, which features the mother of one of his children saying he told her "lasers" from his Starlink satellite network would help get Donald Trump elected in 2024. It came after Berlin artist ANYX released her debut solo album, Starlink, which slams Musk's satellites. On September 24, Musk's fellow Trump-supporting, artificial intelligence-pushing billionaire Larry Ellison said he was using force majeure to protect his new data centre from protesters. Days earlier, Portuguese band The Black Wizards put out their new LP, which skewers such moves. LISTEN>>>

Three days before his force majeure move, Ellison cleared another legal hurdle when his family was allowed to take over Warner Bros and its Trump-resisting news network CNN. The decision came after Trump banned CNN and other unfavourable news networks from the White House on September 18. The same day, US blues musician Seasick Steve released his aptly-named album, The Last Season of America. On its title track he sings: "Whoa, have you come to see the last show? It's the last season of the America that we know." That followed the new LP from The Linda Lindas, whose protest songs went viral in 2021 after they started their band as schoolgirls. On its single "Blood On Our Hands", they take aim at Trump's wars, climate vandalism and tax-dodging "big beautiful bill" with the words: "I don't care about your wealth, I don't care about your tax breaks. Nothing big or beautiful about a fascist state." LISTEN>>>

Legendary rocker Neil Young, whose 2025 song "Big Crime" also called Trump a fascist, released his latest Trump-bashing LP on September 18. On "Soon I Might Be Going", he blasts Trump's destruction as he sings: "Soon I might be going, so I wanted you to know, the sun's sure hot today in Canada, wherever people go. They're looking at the sky like they're waiting for a change. The clouds that used to pour the rain are billowy and strange. He's tearing down the old White House, those days were never olden. The bears are trying to hibernate but can't find where to go. 'Cause everything is different now just like a TV show. author: Emma Black
title: Strangulation: How did attempted murder become normal?
content:
A 16-year-old woman from Sydney’s northern beaches died in hospital in late August after reportedly being strangled during consensual sex with her partner. The tragedy has sparked a long-overdue reckoning with the consequences for young women of the pornification of sex and the normalisation of sexual violence that has come with it.

In recent years, sexual strangulation has gone from being a relatively marginal phenomenon to an everyday sexual practice. In Australia, 61 percent of young women report having been strangled during sex, according to a

2024 survey

 of thousands of 18- to 35-year-olds. Men are most likely to be the stranglers. There is no safe way to strangle someone. According to David Corlett and Marie Crabbe, founders of anti-strangulation advocacy group Breathless:

“Potential 

consequences

 [of strangulation]

range from

 neck pain to loss of bladder and bowel control, headaches, memory loss, seizures, brain damage, stroke and, as seems to be the case with the young woman from the northern beaches, death. The risks and consequences are cumulative, so the more someone is strangled, the more likely they are to suffer harm.”

Only a tiny percentage of middle-aged and older adults have engaged in sexual strangulation, but among young people it’s become commonplace. Maree Crabbe, who is also the director of

It’s Time We Talked

, says strangulation wasn’t an issue before about 2019. But things have changed dramatically since then. “In recent years, we’ve been hearing it’s become normal for young people of all backgrounds, socioeconomic groups, cultures, sexual orientations”, she recently told the

Sydney Morning Herald

.

So how did a potentially deadly act become a normal sexual practice?

The main driver is pornography.

Recent research

 found more than 60 percent of 18- to 35-year-olds had encountered sexual strangulation depicted in pornography. One study comparing the content in the most popular pornography across the two and a half decades to 2024 found that sexual strangulation has gone from almost non-existent to featuring in 15 percent of scenes.

Pornography has become the de facto sex education system for millions of young people. And strangulation is just the latest trend in an industry that maximises profits by selling more extreme depictions of violent and degrading treatment of women.

A landmark 2010 study of best-selling pornographic videos, published in the journal

Violence Against Women

, found that 88 percent contained physical aggression, while 49 percent of scenes contained verbal aggression. Perpetrators were usually male, whereas targets were overwhelmingly female. Targets most often showed pleasure or responded neutrally to the aggression.

So the vast majority of mainstream pornography, whether it depicts strangulation or not, reinforces the idea that violence and humiliation are not only permissible, but pleasurable for women. The pornography industry has “blood on its hands” for propagating this sort of violent content, according to Chanel Contos, founder of

Teach Us Consent

.

An example of how normalised strangulation during sex has become came from this year’s Eurovision song contest.

Romania’s 2026 song entry

 “Choke Me” repeats the words “choke me” 30 times in three minutes. The song also contains the lyrics “It’s hard to breathe in” and “make my lungs explode”.

Many mainstream commentators

emphasise

 the importance of avoiding “kink-shaming” when addressing the issue of sexual strangulation with young people. This dresses up the prioritisation of men’s sexual gratification over women’s safety as sex-positive open-mindedness. And it wilfully ignores the fact that sexual desires and practices are not simply a matter of individual preference; they are shaped and constructed in a society where women are not equal to men, and enormous profit can be made from sex by companies competing for market share.

The reality is that people’s sexual inclinations have not radically changed on their own over the last 50 years, such that the majority of men now enjoy inflicting harm on women. Market forces have pushed things in this direction. In an attempt to be more sensational and attract market share, pornography companies have taken the male-dominant trope that underpins the construction of mainstream heterosexuality and pumped it up to a new extreme. This has shaped attitudes to sex and sexual desire, which in turn further reinforces the business model. And …

title: Nötige Wende in der Lohn- und Einkommenspolitik: Löhne in der Schweiz müssen steigen
content:
Dossier


„

An seiner heutigen Delegiertenversammlung (DV) haben die Delegierten der Schweizerische Gewerkschaftsbund SGB über den wachsenden Lohnrückstand debattiert. Ein grosses Problem sehen die Delegierten bei den zu tiefen Löhnen bei Gelernten. Deshalb wurde eine Resolution für eine Aufwertung der Löhne nach der Lehre und substanzielle Lohnerhöhungen für alle verabschiedet. Wer eine Lehre hat soll mindestens 5’000 Franken im Monat verdienen. (…) Die Reallöhne sind heute nicht wesentlich höher als im Jahr 2016. Es droht ein «verlorenes Jahrzehnt». Hauptgrund ist, dass zahlreiche Arbeitgeber nicht bereit waren, ihren Angestellten den Teuerungsausgleich zu gewähren – obwohl die Produktivität ständig steigt.

Es braucht eine Wende in der Schweizer Lohn- und Einkommenspolitik. Die Reallöhne der Normal- und Geringverdienenden müssen markant stiegen

…“ Aus der

Medienmitteilung vom 31. Mai 2024 des SGB

 

, siehe mehr Informationen:


Schweiz: Je tiefer der Lohn, desto höher die Gesundheitsrisiken


„Immer öfter fehlen Arbeitnehmende am Arbeitsplatz, weil sie krank sind oder einen Unfall hatten. 2010 fehlten Arbeitnehmende im Vollzeitpensum durchschnittlich 6,3 Tage. 2025 waren es bereits 8,1 Tage. In praktisch allen Berufsgruppen stieg die Anzahl der Absenzentage. Es gibt jedoch grosse Unterschiede ­zwischen den Berufen. Während Führungskräfte 2025 fünf Tage ­aufgrund von Krankheit oder Unfall am Arbeitsplatz fehlten und Arbeitnehmende in wissenschaftlichen Berufen knapp sechs Tage, waren es bei Bürokräften, Dienstleistungsberufen und im Detailhandel fast 9,5 Tage. Arbeitnehmende in handwerklichen Berufen fehlten sogar fast 11 Tage, Hilfsarbeiterinnen fast 12 und Bediener von Maschinen über 12 Tage. (…) Diese Zahlen zeigen: Die Absenzen sind in körperlich belastenden Berufen besonders hoch. Dies ist nicht überraschend: Es ist erwiesen, dass physische Belastungen bei der Arbeit, wie etwa das Tragen von Lasten, die Gesundheit der Arbeitnehmenden belasten. Aber auch psychosoziale Belastungen wie Stress und hohe Anforderungen wirken sich negativ auf die Gesundheit aus. Immer mehr Arbeitnehmende sind gestresst, rund 30 Prozent fühlen sich emotional erschöpft. (…) Der Gesundheitsschutz an den Arbeitsplätzen muss verbessert werden, damit die Arbeitnehmenden weniger krank werden. Doch die Bürgerlichen im Parlament wollen genau das Gegenteil: Sie wollen Arbeitszeiten und die Sonntagsarbeit ausweiten und Ruhezeiten einschränken. Das ist ein Angriff auf die Gesundheit der Arbeitnehmenden. Stattdessen sollten die Arbeitszeiten verkürzt werden, damit genügend Zeit für Erholung bleibt…“

(…) Seit Jahren reiten ideologische Arbeitgeber via ihre Parteien Angriff um Angriff auf die Rechte der Arbeitnehmenden. Die Lohnabhängigen sollen 7 Tage die Woche 17 Stunden arbeiten und das am liebsten noch zu Löhnen, die unter dem Existenzminimum liegen. author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Contract nurse questions workers’ compensation denial after she was hit by ATV
content:
A nurse who was struck by an ATV this summer in Gjoa Haven says she won’t return to Nunavut because she feels unsupported by the territorial government and

Workers’ Safety and Compensation Commission.


Teresa Vo uses a walker during rehabilitation at West Park Healthcare Centre in Toronto in July. She is now an outpatient at the health centre. (Photo by Sam Laskaris, special to Nunatsiaq News)


Teresa Vo was in the middle of a four-week nursing contract when she was

walking home

 from a late shift at the hamlet’s health centre on June 18. A child driving an ATV struck her, leaving her with multiple fractures and internal injuries.


She is still in physiotherapy, limited in how far she can walk and unsure when she will be able to work again.


While in recovery, Vo fought a second battle over whether the accident happened during “the Course of Employment” — a technical determination on which thousands of dollars of workers’ compensation payments hinged.


“Dealing with this, feeling like I’ve been thrown under the bus and having to figure all this out on my own, is quite daunting,” she said.


Vo said her nursing contracts did not tell her that an injury while walking between her employer-provided accommodation and her work might not be covered. She also said

she has not received return-to-work support from the GN, such as disability support she received from another employer in the south.


“I believe there is a broader issue here about how remote and northern health-care workers are protected, supported and treated when something goes seriously wrong,” Vo said.


Claim denied, then accepted … then denied again


The Workers’ Safety and Compensation Commission first denied Vo’s claim on July 24. She appealed on Aug. 6, which the commission accepted.


The commission

 paid out $3,783.89 on Sept. 2 for two weeks of missed work.


Then, on Sept. 3, the commission overturned its decision again, citing information provided by the GN, and Vo was asked to repay the money she had received.


The commission sent her another letter on Sept. 17, saying it wouldn’t attempt to recover that initial payment. (WSCC does not recover payments it made if “a previous compensation decision is changed.”)


The claim denial cited a policy that says since Vo

was not on employer premises, no work incident had occurred and the injury did not arise out of and during the course of employment.


Vo disputes this because she was a travelling nurse, living at employer-provided accommodations, and had no other reasonable option to get home. 


She had worked overtime on the night of the incident until about 7:30 p.m. and, because she was not on call, said she could not use one of the two vehicles reserved for nurses who might need to return to the health centre quickly.


She was also unable to hitch a ride with the two other nurses on duty.


Travel insurance helped cover costs associated with her treatment and return south, while Ontario’s public health insurance covered her eligible medical care in Ontario, Vo said.


She hoped WSCC compensation would replace lost income and help pay her mortgage, bills and day-to-day expenses while she cannot work.


‘Employer has a responsibility,’ say labour experts


Christopher McLeod, a University of British Columbia professor and director of the Partnership for Work, Health and Safety, said workers’ compensation systems have traditionally drawn a line between the workplace and a worker’s commute. But that line is more grey in Vo’s case.


“If she was at employer-provided accommodation and going back and forth between her place of work and her accommodation, I think you can make a really strong argument that the employer has a responsibility to ensure that she can get home safely,” McLeod said.


The commission acknowledged the limited infrastructure in Gjoa Haven but said she had completed her shift, was travelling home for personal purposes, was not on call and was not performing work-related duties. Transportation to and from work was not part of Vo’s contract and she was expected to walk, the denial said. Taxis were available if she was uncomfortable walking.


“At the time of the accident, I was travelling directly from my workplace to employer-provided accommodation. This was not an ordinary commute from work to my personal residence,” Vo said in her Aug. 6 email that appealed the decision.


“Taxi service was unreliable to the point that it could not reasonably be depended upon, leaving …

title: Ipek: Looking only at the final link in child worker deaths is wrong - Part Two
content:
Deniz Ipek, a Class A occupational safety expert working with the İSİG Assembly, spoke to ANF about child labour in Turkey and the reasons behind the rising number of worker deaths.


Part one of this interview can be read

here

. 


Child labour is rising in small and informal workplaces


Ipek said child labour is now used in sectors such as industry, construction and textiles, increasing the risk of death and serious injury among children.  Ipek continued: “We cannot explain the increase in child worker deaths solely by a lack of safety measures in workplaces. We need to look at the fact that more children are entering production, working longer hours and performing more dangerous jobs. In the past, child labour was mainly associated with agriculture, small businesses and informal workshops, but today it extends across a wide range of sectors, including industry, construction, logistics, motorcycle delivery, metalwork, textiles and services. MESEM has also made the presence of children in businesses widespread through the education system rather than exceptional. As the number of working children and their exposure to hazards increase, so does the risk of death and serious injury.


A second reason is the nature of the workplaces where child labour is concentrated. Small businesses, industrial estates, agriculture and informal workplaces are among the areas where occupational health and safety measures are weakest. Children work in workplaces where machinery lacks safety guards, electrical installations are unsafe, precautions for working at height are not taken and working hours are long. Within the master-apprentice relationship, performing dangerous tasks is also sometimes regarded as a natural part of ‘learning the job’. Another issue is the child’s lack of power in the workplace. A 15-year-old child cannot object to an employer or master even to the same extent as an adult worker. It is much more difficult for a child to say, ‘I don’t know how to do this,’ ‘This is dangerous,’ or ‘I won’t do it.’ When age, inexperience and workplace authority come together, a child’s ability to protect themselves becomes extremely limited.


That is why it is wrong to look only at the final link in child worker deaths. Before asking, ‘Was there a helmet? Was training provided?’, we need to ask why the child was there, whether the work was appropriate for their age, whether they should have been operating that machine, how long they were working and whether the workplace had previously been inspected. If the child was sent to a workplace through an education programme, the responsibility of the school and public authorities cannot be excluded from the investigation. Deaths also do not show the full health toll of child labour. Loss of fingers and limbs, severe burns, electric shocks, poisoning, musculoskeletal injuries, and exposure to dust and chemicals represent a much broader problem. Today, we do not know how many children are affected by these harms.


Therefore, the increase in child worker deaths cannot be explained solely by individual failures to take precautions in workplaces. The spread of child labour into wider areas of production, increased exposure to hazardous work, the mass placement of children in businesses through models such as MESEM, and inadequate public oversight are all parts of the same picture. The rise in child worker deaths cannot be considered separately from the place of child labour within production relations.”


Inspections are insufficient and workplaces should be visited unannounced


Ipek said workplace inspections in Turkey are neither widespread nor frequent enough and stressed that child labour is concentrated in small workshops and informal businesses. Ipek also said: “Workplaces in Turkey are inspected. The real question is whether inspections are carried out with the reach, frequency and methods needed to reveal the current scale of child labour. What we see on the streets shows that this is not sufficient. If child labour has become so visible in industrial estates, small workshops, agriculture, textiles, services and informal businesses, we cannot be satisfied merely with the existence of legislation.


Child labour is growing particularly in areas that inspections struggle to reach. There are a great many small businesses, informal employment is widespread, and agricultural work is dispersed. MESEM has added a new dimension to this: in some workplaces, a child is no longer simply …
