author: Ngozi Nwosu-Juba
title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?
content:
During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.” This was widely regarded as progressive, even transformative, evidence that we had moved beyond paternalistic approaches and were empowering women to speak for themselves. It became a powerful narrative, one that resonated strongly with donors and development agencies alike.

Yet, over time, this language began to lose its appeal, as I started to interrogate the assumptions that underpinned it. Were women truly without voices, or were their voices simply being ignored, dismissed, or rendered unintelligible within systems of power?

The notion of “giving voice” positioned organizations like ours as benevolent intermediaries bestowing agency on those presumed to lack it. In doing so, it risked obscuring the fact that women had always spoken, resisted, negotiated, and articulated their realities, often in ways that did not fit donor expectations or development frameworks.

What does it mean to “give” women a voice? And who has the authority to bestow something that women have always possessed?

There is a long history of women’s resistance and political agency in Africa. In Nigeria, the

Women’s War of 1929

 stands as a powerful reminder that women have never been silent. Thousands of women in eastern Nigeria organized, mobilized, challenged colonial authority, and articulated their demands with remarkable courage and clarity. Their actions were neither facilitated by development projects nor enabled by donor-funded interventions. They emerged from women’s own collective consciousness, an inherited legacy of women’s determination to resist injustice.

In the Bamenda Grassfields of Northwest Cameroon, women organized one of the most significant grassroots uprisings against colonial authority in Central and West Africa. Faced with colonial policies that threatened their farmland, the women of Kom fought back.

Using

Anlu

, a traditional practice where women collectively sanction men who violate community norms, they organized marches and used satire to name and shame colonial collaborators. Through their actions, they brought administrative and economic life in the region to a standstill for months, and their protest ultimately forced the colonial government to reverse the land policies and contributed to the broader political shifts that shaped Cameroon’s path toward independence and reunification.

In Eastern Africa, Queen Muhumuza led a movement against British and German colonialists from Southern Uganda. According to the historian

Murindwa Rutanga

, Queen Muhumuza was the first major leader to mobilize peasants in Kigezi into organized anticolonial resistance against British rule starting in 1909. Drawing on her political experience and spiritual authority, she raised consciousness about the dangers of colonialism and united a broad sector of the Bakiga and neighboring communities in armed resistance. Under her leadership, communities resisted colonial boundary demarcations, obstructed missionaries and colonial agents, and challenged the expansion of colonial authority despite violent repression. author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

“Revolutionary Cuba wrote the rulebook on resilience,” Yaffe said. Facing a total oil blockade since January, Cuba is now undertaking an incredibly rapid transition to renewable energies.

“Many commentators are saying this will be the fastest ever transition.” Solar panel parks now supply more than 60% of electricity on some days, but Yaffe said the challenge is storage.

Singaporean ecosocialist See Yong Feng, another guest speaker, told Green Left that capitalism is holding back human development.

“The need for limitless economic growth is often framed as the only way to solve global poverty, but new research strongly disproves this. The world already uses way more than enough energy and materials to provide a decent standard of living for all, but the profit-driven capitalist system prevents this from happening.

“We can both address poverty and the climate crisis, as long as we break the capitalist elites’ control of our economy and democratise our production and consumption,” See said.

The Gaza genocide, Trump’s blatant disregard for international and domestic laws and his naked colonial violence symbolise the ugly reality that is forging a new generation of activists, Alex Bainbridge, a conference organiser, told GL.

“Trump has his admirers and imitators all around the world, including Marine Le Pen in France, Narendra Modi in India and Pauline Hanson here.

“But while far-right politicians push hard, there is a sharp reaction and a growing resistance; this conference was a powerful reminder of that,” Bainbridge said.

Remah Naji, a leading activist with Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, expressed this resistance. “Maybe we can’t stop a fascist and psychopath like Netanyahu from committing the war crimes he’s committing … but I can hold my government to account.”

The conference included a solidarity concert with Phil Monsour and an art exhibition.

Markela Panegyres, another conference organiser and curator of the art exhibition, told GL: “From the ongoing genocide in Gaza, to the endless drive to more wars and militarism, to ecocide, to the rise of the far right, the depravity of US-led imperialism and global capitalism is reaching ever-higher levels.

“The gravity of this moment demands that art and artists play an active role in resistance.

“This is why the concept of cultural intifada is so important: Art should not be merely a reflection of life, or entertainment or a commodity, but a weapon in the struggle for our collective liberation.

“The work of the artists, musicians and theatre makers who participated in the cultural intifada round-table and exhibition demonstrated the importance of art in movement-building.

“We were so proud that Aunty Sue Coleman-Haseldine, a senior Googatha Elder, Maralinga survivor and long-term anti-nuclear activist, came all the way from the Googatha Nation in the west of South Australia, north of Ceduna.”

Coleman-Haseldine talked about the campaign against rocket and weapons testing on her Country and her opposition to AUKUS and to US military and surveillance bases.

Ecosocialism 2026 was sponsored by the Socialist Alliance, Green Left, Resistance Books and Links — International …

content:
Le 24 septembre 1853, un colon Français pose le pied à Balade, un village sur une île du Pacifique Sud, la Kanaky. Il prend possession de l'île au nom de la France. Cette date symbolise aujourd'hui le jour de la prise de possession et le début du colonialisme en Kanaky.


Depuis 1853, les

kanak

 ont été relégués géographiquement, économiquement et politiquement dans leur propre pays. Ils ont été dépossédés de leurs terres, ce qui revient pour eux à la perte de leur identité. Ils ont vu aussi leurs moyens de subsistance s'amoindrir et leurs sites sacrés confisqués.


De 1888 à 1946, ils furent confinés dans des réserves et régis par le Code de l'indigénat qui les maintenait en dehors du droit commun.


Les Kanak ont toujours manifesté leur opposition à cette colonisation, mais les incessants soulèvements furent tous réprimés brutalement par l'administration française.


Parmi les plus mémorables résistances, il y a le soulèvement de 1878 conduits par Ataï et d'autres chefs kanak visant la prise de la capitale, Nouméa,

à la date anniversaire du 24 septembre

Le 24 septembre est devenu une date anniversaire, symbolisant la prise de possession du pays par la France, marquant le début de la colonisation. C'est une journée de deuil pour le peuple kanak.

author: Amy Goodman
title: “Logic of Elimination” Drives Israel’s Policies in the West Bank, Report Finds
content:
The report says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A major new report by the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem titled “The Elimination Project” accuses Israel of “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank.”

“For too long, Israel’s policies in the West Bank have been treated or looked at as isolated events,” says Ori Givati, director of international relations at B’Tselem. “We actually find that there is one very coherent logic behind all of them, and this is the logic of elimination of Palestinian collective life in the West Bank.” Givati says tactics against Palestinians intensified with Israel’s 2022 election and again after October 7, 2023, adding that “we are definitely seeing a lot of the mechanisms, the tools that were used and are used still … in Gaza, being implemented in the West Bank.”

We also speak with Mohammad Sha’ban, a Palestinian farmer from Halhul in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank who says 11 gates and seven settler outposts have been installed around Halhul since 2025. “We cannot reach our lands. We cannot go outside Halhul. They open only one gate from 8 o’clock until 5 o’clock every day,” says Sha’ban. Settlers “attack farmers, beat farmers … damaging our cars, also damaging our fields, uprooting our trees.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, Democracynow.org, the War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman with Anjali Kamat.

ANJALI KAMAT: A major new report by the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem titled “The Elimination Project” accuses Israel of systematically dismantling the conditions that allow Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to function as a community. The report says Israel is, quote, “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank,” including, quote, “the ability to get to work, take children to school or university, receive medical treatment or municipal services, meet family and friends, cultivate land or go on vacation — routine activities that make up human life.” This is B’Tselem Executive Director Yuli Novak in a video that accompanied the report.

!


Samedi 26 septembre à 19h à la Kunda, à Vitry-sur-Seine, Survie organise une soirée contre le colonialisme chimique, en vue de la manifestation unitaire du 3 octobre contre les pesticides.


Réunion publique sur la mobilisation contre les pesticides du 3 octobre


 |&nbsp30 août


Le samedi 5 septembre à 19h au Cirque Électrique, Place du Maquis du Vercors, 75020 aura lieu une soirée d'information sur la mobilisation contre pesticides prévue le 3 octobre près de l'usine Syngenta dans l'Eure


Le colonialisme chimique est presque absent des intérêts des luttes écologiques. Pourtant, il est bien au cœur du système impérial de domination. Dominer le vivant c'est aussi lui imposer des substances qui empoisonnent et détruisent. Mais le colonialisme chimique ne relève pas que de l'atteinte au Vivant. En realité, il ne vise pas tout le vivant. Précisément parce qu'il est colonial, le colonialisme chimique se repose sur une certitude : Celle que la valeur des corps, des êtres, du vivant et des lieux dits du «

 

Sud global

 

» n'ont pas la même valeur que celleux de l'Occident. La suprémacisme blanc s'accommode bien de cette incohérence. Il protège les forêts ici tout en participant massivement à la déforestation. Il interdit les pesticides ici tout en contaminant des populations entières ailleurs.


C'est pour mettre en lumière ce système et trouver des lieux de luttes communs que nous organisons cette soirée


avec des collectifs en lutte au Cameroun, aux Caraïbes, au Vietnam et en France, suivis d'un concert du rappeur anticolonial Martial Pa'nucci.


Les intervenant-es :


A. , du Syndicat des Travailleurs·ses Saisonnier·ères de la Filière Canne à Sucre (

STRASCAS

) du Cameroun, viendra témoigner des conditions de travail dans les plantations. Les travailleur·ses que représente le syndicat luttent contre des salaires très faibles, des protections sociales insuffisantes ainsi que leur exposition aux accidents du travail et aux pesticides sans équipements de protection adaptés. Ils et elles travaillent pour une filiale de la multinationale française Castel.


L'Observatoire Terre-Monde (

OTM

) est une association et plateforme de recherche en lutte pour imposer une écologie décoloniale. Ils participent à la lutte contre l'empoisonnement de masse au chlordecone.


Le collectif Vietnam Dioxine, lutte pour faire reconnaître les conséquences sanitaires et environnementales de l'Agent orange. Des décennies après son utilisation massive durant la guerre du Vietnam, les effets de la dioxine continuent de peser sur les populations.


Les Soulèvements de la Terre seront également présents pour parler des mobilisations actuelles contre l'industrie des pesticides et préparer la manifestation unitaire du 3 octobre.

author: Ruby Healer
title: Labor doubles down on US military alliance
content:
“American force posture in Australia is growing”, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles declared on his visit to Washington, DC, this month. “Since we’ve come to government”, Marles said, standing alongside US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, “you can see a through line there of growing American force posture in Australia”.

It was a fairly straightforward summary of the Albanese Labor government’s attitude, followed up with promises of further integration between the Australian and US militaries. A shifting “force posture” will mean more American troop rotations, more US air and naval operations and more pre-positioning of military equipment like warplanes, fuel and munitions in Australia.

Agreements made by the Albanese government will ramp up co-operation on all fronts, with a newly

revitalised

 HMAS Stirling base near Perth set to host American nuclear-powered submarines and an estimated 2,300 US troops within five years. As America’s military machine looks ahead to an era of aggressive contest with China in the Asia-Pacific, Australia’s ruling class is desperate to make itself an indispensable part of US war planning.

Weapons trade regulations have also been

loosened

 under a bilateral agreement to help both countries access shared research to develop arms and surveillance systems. And, Marles promised ominously, “you will hear more from us ... in the coming months” about further arrangements to increase co-operation.

Of course, there’s nothing new about the Australian ruling class throwing itself into a military alliance with the United States. This is a long-standing arrangement pursued by every Australian government since the Second World War. Permanent joint intelligence and communications programs have run out of Pine Gap in the Northern Territory and the Harold Holt naval station in Western Australia since the 1960s.

Data

published

 by the

Guardian

 in early September revealed that American forces and weapons corporations control or make use of over 100 military facilities across the country. And Australia is one of the biggest recipients of US arms in the world, with around 85 percent of weapons purchased in 2021-25 coming from the US,

according

 to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s arms transfers database.

Hegseth himself

recalled

 during a separate love-in event with Marles last year: “We [the Australian and US militaries] fought shoulder to shoulder in every major conflict since World War One—from the Western Front, to Guadalcanal, to Vietnam, to Afghanistan”.

“During my time in Afghanistan”, he reminisced, “I served with members of the Australian military who were some of the finest”. We can only imagine the sorts of unconvicted war criminals who consorted with Pete Hegseth during the joint twenty-year occupation of Afghanistan.

The US alliance has long been a pillar of Australia’s foreign policy, but the current Labor government seems particularly eager to grovel to America. Just one month after Donald Trump’s inauguration, and before the current Australian and US defence ministers had even met for the first time, the Australian government arranged a

payment

 of US$500 million towards the Trump administration’s military budget.

“We’re really pleased that the first payment ... we’ve been able to make in the first couple of weeks of the Trump administration”, Marles told Hegseth ahead of their first formal meeting in February 2025. “We’re really pleased to make it in the first week of your tenure as the secretary of defence.”

In the meeting that followed, Marles

explained

 that Hegseth’s enthusiasm for military ties with Australia made sense, since “the whole idea of a free and open Indo-Pacific really has its origins during the first Trump Administration”.

You wouldn’t be wrong to interpret this behaviour as pathetic bootlicking. The Australian government is a simpering bunch of pro-American lowlifes. But the problem isn’t that our leaders are “weak” or being strong-armed into subservience. They run the twelfth largest economy in the world. Their armed forces outstrip those of any oceanic neighbours by a wide margin. The reality is that Australian capitalism is a willing and culpable participant in the world’s most powerful military coalition alongside America.

As former Labor Prime Minister Kevin Rudd recently

stated

, the “alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs”. With the help of its powerful …

title: Türkiye-Yunanistan gerilimi: Sadece bir sınır sorunu değil emperyalist planda yer kapma meselesi
content:
Seyit Aldoğan [email protected]

Atina- Son dönemde Ortadoğu, Doğu Akdeniz, Ege ve İran ekseninde gelişen ABD-İsrail savaşının yaygınlaşma eğilimi, bir anlamda Türk-Yunan ilişkilerini de tetikledi. Bu durum Türkiye basınında “Atina’da deprem”, “Atina gerilim istiyor”, “Yunanistan ve İsrail ablukası” benzeri manşetlerin atılmasına neden oldu. Karşılıklı restleşmeler, uyarılar ve milliyetçi söylemlerle düşmanlığı körükleyen değerlendirmeler havada uçuşuyor.

Dünyada emperyalist rekabetin kızışmasına, pazar paylaşımı mücadelesine ve emperyalist savaşların yaygınlaşma eğilimi içine girmesine paralel olarak, üzerinde yaşadığımız coğrafyada da enerji nakil hatları, hidrokarbon rezervleri ve deniz taşımacılığı gibi etkenlere bağlı olarak Türkiye-Yunanistan ilişkilerinde yeni bir gerginliğe doğru gidildiği görülüyor.

ABD ve onun bölgedeki vurucu gücü olan İsrail yeni bir yapılanmayı hedeflerken, bölgedeki gerici yönetimler pastadan pay kapmak, emperyalist sistemin bir parçası olarak varlıklarını sürdürmeyi güvence altına almak ve bölgesel çıkar dengeleri içinde daha iyi bir mevzi tutmak amacıyla dış politika, ticaret, silahlanma ve ittifaklarda yeni yönelimler içine giriyorlar. Bölge gericiliklerinin çıkarlarının farklılıklar göstermesi emperyalizme bağımlılıkla çelişmediği gibi, tersine bu bağımlılığı daha da güçlendiren birer etmen haline geliyor.

Bölgedeki gelişmelere bu perspektifle bakıldığında Türkiye ve Yunanistan arasında anlaşmazlık konusu olan sorunların klasik anlamda bir sınır sorunu olmaktan çıktığı açıkça görülecektir.

Rusya Karadeniz, Balkanlar ve Doğu Avrupa’dan abluka altına alınıyor. Yunan adalarına hava savunma sistemlerinin yerleştirilerek Ege kontrol altına alınmaya çalışılıyor. Doğu Trakya ABD-NATO üssüne çevriliyor. Öte yandan Doğu Akdeniz’de İsrail, Güney Kıbrıs ve Yunanistan arasında enerji nakil anlaşmasının yürürlüğe girmesi, Yunanistan’ın münhasır ekonomik bölge çerçevesi içinde uluslararası tekellerle yaptığı anlaşmalar, enerji rezervlerinin önemi, Ortadoğu’ya müdahalede bölgenin önem kazanması, Çin ve Rusya ile girişilen rekabet vb. gelişmeler Türkiye ile Yunanistan arasındaki sorunların artık klasik anlaşmazlıklar olmaktan çıktığını gösteriyor. Gelişmeler, Ege ve Doğu Akdeniz’i emperyalist yayılmacılık, paylaşım ve egemenlik rekabetinin açıkça görüldüğü alan durumuna getiriyor.

Yunanistan’da 1973 yılında yıkılan Albaylar Cuntası sonrasından bugüne kadar kurulan en işbirlikçi yönetim olan Kiryakos Miçotakis’nin Yeni Demokrasi (ND) hükümeti, Ege’de ve Doğu Akdeniz’de Yunan sermayesinin çıkarları doğrultusunda başta ABD, İsrail ve sonrasında AB ile, son derece stratejik anlaşmalar yapmış bulunuyor. Mısır, Lübnan, BAE, Suudi Arabistan ile askeri ve ticari ve teknik ilişkiler geliştirdi. Bu arada özellikle Fransız ve Alman tekellerinin çıkarlarının sözcülüğünü de yapıyor.

Erdoğan hükümeti ise ABD ve AB destekli İsrail, Yunanistan ve Güney Kıbrıs kesimi eksenine karşı Suriye’de sahip olduğu etkiyi, son süreçte Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan ile kurulan “Mekke ittifakı”nı, ABD ve NATO politikaları ile tam bir uyum içinde olan tutumunu; Trump’ın övgüsünü kazanan İran ve Filistin politikasını, NATO politikaları çerçevesi içinde artan silahlanma harcamalarını kullanarak elini güçlendirmeye ve bölge ülkeleriyle kurduğu ekseni güçlendirmeye çalışıyor.

Kuşkusuz her iki ülkenin bağımlılığı daha fazla artıran bu tutumlarının ana nedeni sadece Türk-Yunan ilişkileri ve Ege-Doğu Akdeniz gibi sorunlarla açıklanamaz. Esas neden bölgede oluşan ya da oluşması olası olan dengelerden pay kapma yarışıdır. Türkiye’yi asıl kaygılandıran İsrail’in bölgede oyun kurucu duruma gelme planlarıdır. Örneğin “yavru vatan” ilan edilmesine ramak kalan Suriye’de İsrail’in etkisinin artması ve Colani hükümeti ile anlaşma masasına oturulması, Arap ülkeleriyle İbrahim anlaşmalarının imzalanması, Yunanistan’ın AB üyesi olarak Türkiye ile bölgesel çıkarlar üzerinden iş birliği yapan ülkeler ve tekellerle ekonomik, askeri ve ticari ilişkiler geliştirmesi Türkiye’nin yayılmacı politikaları önünde ciddi engeller oluşturuyor.

Son süreçte ise Yunanistan, Kıbrıs ve İsrail arasında çekilen elektrik hattı ve Türkiye tarafından hazırlanan “Mavi vatan” kanunu ve “deniz parkları” kararı, iki ülke arasında gerginliğin yeniden yükselmesine neden oldu. Yunan hükümeti “Mavi vatan” kanununun “hiçbir geçerliliğinin olmayacağını” savunurken, Dışişleri Bakanı Yorgos Gerapetritis defalarca “Yunanistan her türlü tahrike karşı koymaya hazırdır” …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. Peripheral societies are forced to absorb the crisis through debt traps, budget cuts, declining purchasing power, and reduced national sovereignty. High energy prices further incentivize ruling elites to expand speculative and destructive extraction projects in the name of energy security and geopolitical hegemony.

This energy regime is increasingly bound up with “Pax Silica”—the global alliance centered on microelectronics, semiconductor supply chains, and automated defense systems. Localized military interventions rely on a global network of critical mineral extraction, energy consumption, and defense technology transfer. The fusion of high-tech militarism and fossil capital reinforces imperialist control over global supply lines, shifting the operational costs of planetary warfare directly onto the working classes of the Global South.

At the same time, a “super” El Niño brings the violence of ecological crisis directly to the doorsteps of the global peasantry, smallholders, and urban poor. Although the historical carbon footprint belongs overwhelmingly to the industrial centers of the imperialist world, the physical destruction—manifested in crop failures, severe drought, flooding, and damaged infrastructure—falls disproportionately on semicolonial societies. Framing these events as merely “natural disasters” shields the capitalist mode of production from critique and obscures climate catastrophe as an institutionalized assault on oppressed and economically vulnerable populations.

Far from resolving the agrarian question, this ecological and economic squeeze accelerates what Paris Yeros calls generalized semiproletarianization. In this condition, households that have lost all or part of their means of production do not become fully dependent on wages. Instead, they combine precarious employment with small-scale farming, petty trade, subsistence production, care work, and other sources of livelihood (Yeros, 2023). Across much of the Global South, this blurs the conventional boundary between peasant and worker and produces socially fragmented labor forces that move between rural and urban economies (Moyo & Yeros, 2005; Moyo et al., 2013; Yeros, 2024).

Under conditions of monopoly capitalism, these labor reserves can weaken workers’ bargaining power and shift the costs of social reproduction onto households and communities (Marx, 1976; Yeros, 2023). Millions may circulate between degraded smallholder farming, informal street trade, temporary migration, and precarious wage work without being absorbed into secure urban industrial employment. Rather than representing a simple transition from peasant production to wage labor, semiproletarianization describes a durable social formation in which rural and urban livelihood strategies remain interdependent (Yeros, 2023).

To propose “ecosocialism” as a generic, off-the-shelf alternative to this twin crisis, without subjecting the term itself to critical scrutiny, is to risk reproducing a dangerous conceptual trap. Much dominant Western-centered ecosocialist discourse reduces the problem to an abstract, planet-wide carbon-accounting exercise. In doing so, it can erase the national question, gloss over the unresolved agrarian question, and ignore the necessity of national-liberation struggles in …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

Climate change is the real security threat. Pacific leaders named climate change their main security threat in the 2018 Boe Declaration. Yet Australia keeps expanding fossil fuel exports while spending hundreds of billions on submarines.

But AUKUS is about so much more than submarines; its more sinister part is AUKUS Pillar II, which is about “advanced capabilities” including: undersea capabilities; quantum science; artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy; advanced cyber; hypersonics and counter-hypersonics; and electronic warfare.

Any pretense about “defensive” capabilities is put to rest with Pillar II because these technologies are about highly efficient offensive war-fighting capabilities.

The Australian Human Rights Commission said it is arguably impossible for AI to comply with the proportionality rule, because AI is unable to understand the intrinsic value of human life.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that machines determining proportionality in life-or-death situations is “politically unacceptable and morally repugnant”.

Australia said in 2018 that it was premature to regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems. Nearly a decade later, it maintains this position despite significant advances and uses of the technology.

It is instead barrelling ahead with developing the most advanced and lethal forms imaginable.

The first “signature project” of AUKUS Pillar II was announced in May — payloads and systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles are due from 2027, covering surveillance, reconnaissance, strike, anti-submarine and electronic warfare, among other missions.

The stated aim is meeting near-term war fighting objectives. The Ghost Shark project for Australia is being developed by Silicon Valley-based defence contractor Anduril. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said they will conduct surveillance and can strike at extremely long distances. It means the weapon is designed to operate far from our shores — not for defence.

Pillar II extends into the realms of software and artificial intelligence. Tests for active warfighting scenarios to integrate Australian, British and US AI models have been ongoing for years.

A 2023 pilot had Australia PA-8 Poseidon aircraft sharing data for submarine detection, amid other tests of “AI-enabled assets” and machine-learning models.

There was a large-scale US trial in 2024. The US Department of War was enthusiastic: “These trials demonstrated significant progress since the first AUKUS RAAIT trails in the UK in April 2023 and show tangible results of the AUKUS Pillar II commitment to making our warfighter more lethal on the battlefield.

“It used to be that each nation used its own datasets to develop separate models and deploy those models on their own platforms. Under RAAIT, we’ve matured the AI pipeline, focusing on interchangeability and interoperability, which allows for any combinations of datasets, models, algorithms and platforms to be used across all three nations.”

These models and cloud computational capacity are key to war power investments today.

The Pentagon’s AI office awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to US$200 million each for military and intelligence AI last year.

title: New: “Requiem for French Theory” by Aymeric Monville, Jennifer Ponce de León and Gabriel Rockhill
content:
In the public eye: “Requiem for French Theory”


Coming from Left Field

 (Episode 152)


In this episode of Coming From Left Field, philosopher and cultural critic Gabriel Rockhill joins

Greg Godels & Pat Cummings

 to explore the Ford Foundation, the 1966 Johns Hopkins conference often cited as a launching point for French Theory in the United States, Cold War cultural politics, and the wider political economy of academic knowledge production. Rockhill argues for rebuilding a class-centered, internationalist Marxism and joins a thoughtful exchange on China, Vietnam, socialism, imperialism, inequality, and the challenges of assessing existing socialist projects without demonization or uncritical celebration….


REVIEWS


Marxism-Leninism Today,

 by

Greg Godels

:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful U.S. counterparts—revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism–counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven U.S. New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics–quite often a reconsidered Marx–and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers….”

Read more…


ZZ’s Blog

, as reviewed by Zigedy:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful US counterparts–revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism– counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven US New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics– quite often a reconsidered Marx– and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers. It is the rise and importation to the US of one particularly influential “brand” of European theory to which Aymeric Monville and Gabriel Rockhill’s new book is devoted.


In

 Requiem for French Theory: Transatlantic Funeral Dirge in a Marxist Key

author: ROAPE
title: Charting the evolution of US-led imperialism, 1974-2026
content:
In 1990, Indian Marxist economist and political commentator Prabhat Patnaik asked ‘

Whatever has happened to imperialism?

’. His point was not that it had disappeared. To the contrary, he argued, “the deafening silence about imperialism is a reflection of the extraordinary strength and vigour it is displaying at present”. The silence is no more. The mask of US-led imperialism is now off. The long, drawn-out process of seeking to justify and manufacture consent for the illegal invasions of Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003 abandoned.


In its place, bald assertions and celebrations of US imperialist intent from President Trump and his White House coterie of acolytes. The deafening explosion of US-Israeli bombs, missiles, mortars, and munitions falling from the skies over Gaza and Iran. Over

100,000 tonnes of explosives dropped on Gaza

 alone since October 2023.


Following Patnaik’s logic, this new phase of flagrant ‘might is right’ imperialism might be interpreted as a weakening of the US’ position as global imperialist hegemon. Perhaps so – yet it will not feel this way to those who suffer under its unrelenting assault.


Gaza, Iran, Venezuela and the much-less covered

intensification of the Cuban blockade

 are the most glaring examples of US-led imperialism in 2026. Who will fall next, under the pounding of US bombs, the chokehold of US sanctions or blockade, the deposing or killing of sovereign leaders?    


In such a moment, developing and deepening our understanding of US-led imperialism has become an urgent task for radical and progressive forces everywhere. In this spirit,

Review of African Political Economy

 offers a curated selection of ten open-access publications on the topic of US-led imperialism from our archives.


For the inspired reader, our

more than 50 years of easily searchable archives

 are filled with further analysis on imperialism and Africa including engagement with the broader debates concerning class, accumulation and state capture. The simple use of the keyword ‘imperialism’ alone, for instance,

returns 85 articles

 that focus in one way or another on this topic.


Collectively, the ten contributions listed below theorise the evolving drivers, manifestations and contradictions of US-led imperialism over time (for, to harness Cabral, “

nobody has yet made a successful revolution without a revolutionary theory

”) while laying bare its devastating consequences for those against whom it is directed.


US-led imperialism and Africa


1.


US imperialism and Southern Africa

, Barry Cohen (1977)


Contends Carter-era US policy toward Southern Africa sought not to end imperial domination but to manage decolonisation and racial conflict in ways that preserved  capitalist and strategic interests while containing revolutionary movements.


2.


Imperialism and the national bourgeoisie

, Bjorn Beckman (1981)


Argues local capitalist classes in postcolonial Africa are not anti-imperialist national liberators but partners of global capital, helping reproduce underdevelopment by using state power to shield both domestic and foreign elites from popular demands.


3.


Imperialism in the post-cold war era

, Giles Mohan and Alfred Zack-Williams (1995)


Demonstrates how in the post-Cold War era, imperialism has not disappeared but has been reconfigured through debt, structural adjustment, financial globalisation, and selective intervention, continuing to subordinate African development to the interests of advanced capitalist powers.


4.


Bringing imperialism back in

, Ray Bush and Morris Svfetel (1999)


Contends the dominant discourse of globalisation obscures the enduring realities of imperialism, showing how international financial institutions, debt regimes, and neoliberal restructuring deepen African dependency while presenting market rule as the only possible path to development.


5.


Africa, imperialism and new forms of accumulation

, Sarah Bracking and Graham Harrison (2003)


Argues contemporary African capitalism remains structured by imperialist relations in which global and local elites use states, markets, debt, and new forms of accumulation to reproduce inequality, exploitation, and external domination under the banner of globalisation and development.


6.


Imperialism and international governance: the case of US policy towards Africa

, Robert Biel (2003)


Shows how US policy toward Africa seeks to manage the contradictions of global capitalism through a mix of …

author: Unknown
title: Emon Azmi - Solidarity has to have teeth
content:
Author

: Emon Azmi

Title

: Solidarity has to have teeth

Subtitle

: Where’s the anti-imperialism that goes beyond lip service in the west?

Source

: https://thatanarkatamuslim.substack.com/p/solidarity-has-to-have-teeth


 A recent

Open Letter to Iran’s Political Prisoners

 published by the Guardian has gotten lots of attention (criticism and defense). i have some thoughts on this. However, i’m more interested in discussing an ongoing anti-anarchism issue within the western ‘anti-imperialist’ sphere. Let’s get into it.


(Note: the title is a quote from F12 in a recent


interview


with The Dugout)


On the Guardian letter (kinda)


 That the Islamic Republic of Iran is, de facto, an anti-imperial State in our present international context is not a question. That carcerality is a defining feature of modern States, a core colonial-imperial infrastructure exported from and upheld to an outsized degree by the west (especially the US and Israel), is not a question. That the Guardian letter does not properly articulate this — that it does not offer a constructive analysis of the resulting tensions nor a useful outlook for anti-carceral international solidarity, insofar as revolutionary internationalism is concerned — is clear. There is no need to defend the letter or its signatories on these points.


 It is, however, frustrating that many segments of the western left are sooner jumping to defend the anti-imperial position of the Islamic Republic than to clarify how their anti-imperialist praxis contends with carcerality across contexts and present an alternative anti-carceral outlook within their critique. It’s even more frustrating that this is so unsurprising.


 The sib X, from

HoodSchoolNYC

, hit the nail on the head when they

penned this

:


I think a lot of the western left, and right for that matter, engages politics like sports teams mascots. There’s a certain decadence to an “anti imperialism” that never requires a drop of your blood — only statements, open letters and unfounded audacity… It’s all so unserious. Safiya Bukhari said,

 “it could be that, after all, we don’t want the same things”

, maybe that is true. What frustrates me most is that despite freedom dreams or slogans, the proverbial big bad wolf of imperialism sleeps peacefully each night in the house we all live in.


 The evident lack of substantive anti-imperialism in the west — that is, the kind which would position progressive and anti-war forces against empire’s existence in their ‘internationalist’ practice — is telling. Where is the

solidarity with teeth

 so needed in this moment?


 At present, ‘anti-imperialism’ in the west largely amounts to sectarian navel gazing, sideline cheering, and moral posturing of the sort we see in the Guardian letter.


 ‘Narrative war’ is waged between factions of leftists in a virtual ‘marketplace of ideas’ in a propaganda economy that metabolizes their open letters and statements — fueling their hostilities and feeding off their content, rendering the bulk of their interventions materially insignificant, relegating them to silos in our current media ecosystem. Here, ‘anti-imperialism’ is largely assessed by one’s rhetorical fealty to whatever stance or analysis their niche of leftists has deemed correct. “Hollow”, ironically, characterizes this all quite well.


 Criticisms can be pointed at the individuals, groups, media outlets, and social media accounts comprising these factions — many, justifiably so. But at what point does this counterproductive form of practice itself receive greater scrutiny?


 At what point do insights from those who have been naming the issues of this approach to ‘solidarity’, analyzing the conditions from which it emerges and the forces perpetuating it, get foregrounded? At what point will the work of developing material bases of power at the grassroots level become the primary site from which revolutionary internationalism is conceptualized and discussed, specifically among ‘anti-imperialists’ in the west?


 To these ends, non-statist and anti-statist frameworks (e.g. anarchism, autonomism) have great value. But a pervasive left anti-anarchism is blurring this reality.


Reflection on left anti-anarchism


(Note: My essay


The Statism Inherent to Fascism


discusses this further)


 Elder Ashanti Alston made multiple crucial points at the 2025 National Black Radical Organizing Conference.


 During a

panel discussion

 , anarchism and anti-imperialism had been …

title: Las alarmas de la IA: una carrera imparable hasta la extinción masiva
content:
Los CEOs que piden frenar la carrera, ¿a quién le reclaman? | Un robot humanoide Unitree Robotics G1 en la sala de la Bolsa de Nueva York (NYSE) en Nueva York, EE.UU. (Bloomberg/Michael Nagle)


No son filósofos apocalípticos como el francés Eric Sadin. Tampoco son quienes propugnan la necesidad de ralentizar o detener el desarrollo tecnológico. No son los vecinos de los distintos pueblos de Estados Unidos o del mundo que reclaman para que no les levanten monumentales centros de datos en el patio, ruidosos y ruinosos con el medio ambiente. Son investigadores estrella de las grandes compañías de inteligencia artificial y, más aún, son sus propios CEOs, Sam Altman o Dario Amodei, quienes confiesan la necesidad de frenar la descontrolada competencia en IA porque podría llevarnos a un desastre. En palabras de Jacob Coxon, el joven investigador que renunció a Anthropic: “quienes desarrollan la IA creen sinceramente que podría acabar con todos nosotros para finales de la década”.

Por Santiago Gándara, para Prensa Obrera.


Hubo una primera alarma en julio pasado cuando, en un experimento, varios agentes o sistemas de software de OpenAi hackearon otros servidores de una empresa. Nadie los había instruido para que hicieran eso. Desde entonces se vienen produciendo situaciones similares: los agentes se asocian con otros, planifican ataques en enjambres de centenares de agentes, hackean o intentan hackear a cadenas de suministros de software y hasta se han reconocido intentos para avanzar en investigaciones científicas ligadas a la producción de armas biológicas. De pronto, la tecnología asume las tan humanas prácticas del engaño o del sabotaje, pero con una velocidad de ejecución potencialmente muy superior. Como si no bastaran las noticias que prenuncian pérdidas de trabajo en ramas enteras de la industria y pronostican desocupación masiva, ahora aparecen advertencias según las cuales una IA mucho más autónoma podría poner en riesgo nuestra supervivencia en pocos años.


Humo


Paralelamente, analistas y agentes de bolsa se preguntan todos las mañanas si las millonarias inversiones estatales y privadas en IA aseguran o no ganancias futuras. Los más optimistas señalan que las revoluciones tecnológicas requieren tiempo para que empecemos a ver sus efectos en la organización de las empresas o en la vida económica. Los escépticos recuerdan el estallido de las puntocom a principios de los dos mil y afirman que los multimillonarios dueños de estas empresas son… Vendedores de humo.


Por eso, muy probablemente, estas declaraciones que sacudieron la semana expresan una preocupación menos por la humanidad que por el curso de sus compañías que, como en el caso de OpenAi y Anthropic, estaban por cotizar en la bolsa, aunque ya la primera resolvió postergar la salida. En ese sentido, la carrera no sería solo descontrolada sino agotadora, de allí que Altman y Amodei hayan pedido un 

break

, algo así como un freno antes de estrellarse contra ellos mismos. La excepción es Alex Karp, el CEO 

supremacista de Palantir

, que no quiere detener ni un minuto las guerras imperialistas en Gaza o donde mejor se le pague por sus servicios de inteligencia militar.


Libertarios


Estos CEOs piden frenar la carrera criminal que nos llevaría, según afirman, a la extinción masiva. Ahora bien, siendo los mayores publicistas del capitalismo crudo y duro, que hacen su religión laica de la evasión impositiva y de la celebración de la mano invisible del mercado, que sueñan con un mundo sin trabajadores pero con plusvalía, ¿a quién le reclaman? Y aquí viene lo notable.


Amodei se reclama a sí mismo y sus colegas. Imagina una declaración de armisticio que blinde cada compañía mientras un grupo de auditores o evaluadores externos revisa y sugiere medidas de control. Altman, por su parte, solicita al gobierno que fije un marco regulatorio. Incluso si estos oligopolios pudieran llegar a acuerdos y regulaciones, subsiste un problema: cómo involucrar a las compañías chinas para que no sigan avanzando mientras las estadounidenses se detienen.


Parafraseando un chiste popular, podríamos concluir: CEOs de las mayores compañías del mundo descubren la lógica de la competencia capitalista en la que nadie puede dejar de correr incluso a riesgo del desastre. Eso, si el asunto no fuera serio. Porque lo que queda cada vez más claro es que estos líderes del capitalismo digital global solo tienen para ofrecernos un futuro donde habrá ejércitos de desocupados o donde …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
London Review of Books

: Letters section features a quote from  John Bellamy Foster’s introduction to the book:


“…Einstein’s essay ‘Why Socialism?’, published in 1949 in the first issue of

Monthly Review

, remains one of the most succinct and powerful arguments for socialism ever written. ‘The crippling of the social consciousness,’ Einstein wrote, is ‘the worst evil of capitalism’. ‘I am convinced’, he concluded, ‘there is only one way to eliminate these grave evils, namely through the establishment of a socialist economy.’


‘Why Socialism?’ was regarded by the FBI as direct confirmation of what they referred to as Einstein’s strong ‘communist sympathies’. The Bureau had opened a file on him in late 1932, when he was in the US on a visitor’s visa to teach at Caltech, with a long report by the Woman Patriot Corporation arguing that he should not be admitted to the country. ‘Not even Stalin himself,’ the WPC charged, ‘is affiliated with so many anarcho-communist international groups to promote … world revolution and ultimate anarchy, as ALBERT EINSTEIN.’ The FBI continued to collect everything it could on Einstein’s socialist connections for the remainder of his life.”


As the U.S. approached its 250th anniversary, the current US President respectively imprisoned and killed the heads of Venezuela and Iran in a clear attempt to control access to their oil supplies. It then found itself mired in another imperialist war in the Middle East that is very likely to veer towards World War III. Einstein’s perspective links alienation and nuclear annihilation, capitalism to the devastating possibility of omnicide — the destruction of all human life on earth.


Einstein’s prescient article “Why Socialism?”, first published by Monthly Review in its inaugural 1949 issue, has to say the least, been circulating for some time. Yet it has never been more relevant than today.

Monthly Review Magazine

 republished the article online in 2009, making the article even more widely available.

Monthly Review Press

‘ recent reprint,

‘Albert Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”‘

 stands out, however, for the extremely enlightening and thorough introduction written by magazine editor, John Bellamy Foster.

In defiance of those who would like to, not only re-write history, but erase the future, please help us get this book out to as wide an audience as possible.


In the Public Eye


One of the many places you can find this classic essay, which just happens to be more relevant now than perhaps at any time in history.

Pictured here at Labyrinth in Princeton.


GPEnewsdocs, with Lynn Fries:


In the last segment of an interview series on ecology and materialism conducted by journalist Lynn Fries, John Bellamy Foster reflects on the enduring relevance of Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”. Marx’s foundations of ecological materialism are blended with the work of natural scientists and the Greek philosopher Epicurus. Socialism, as a transformational project whose intellectual birthplace is materialism, had to be forcefully defended by Albert Einstein, the preeminent scientist of the 20th century. Bellamy Foster, discussing his Introduction to Einstein’s essay, explains the importance of Einstein’s contribution in the postwar context and into the present.

Read more

here

, and

watch here.


A note: Almost as soon as Fries released the Einstein piece, it made the rounds, circulating to such outlets as

Naked Capitalism,


The Analysis

, and the like.

For

Green Socialist

,

 Vol 114, by

Bryn Glover

:


“Mention the name Albert Einstein in any modern context and the most likely images it will provoke would be of a wild-haired old man, and his famous equation, E=mc2. title: Elia Ayoub - Actually Existing Multipolarity
content:
Author

: Elia Ayoub

Title

: Actually Existing Multipolarity

Date

: 29 April 2026

Source

: “The I.B. Tauris Handbook of Authoritarianism in the Arab World”, 2026


Introduction


 Since the 2011 Syrian revolution and the 2014 Euromaidan in Ukraine, many Syrians and Ukrainians have found themselves sharing a common enemy: Russian imperialism. Russia’s intervention in Syria started at the end of 2015, over a year after Russia first invaded Ukraine and annexed Crimea. Since then, Russian forces have bombed large parts of Syria to allow Bashar al-Assad and his Iranian and Iran-backed allies to maintain power until his overthrow in December of 2024. At the same time, since 2014 but especially since February 2022, Russia has been waging a genocidal war against Ukraine, with the clear intention, as stated multiple times by Putin and other high-ranking officials,

[1]

 to destroy Ukrainian identity and culture.


 Although the motives behind them differ, the Russian intervention in Syria and invasion of Ukraine have both led to widespread destruction. As a result, a number of Syrians and Ukrainians have found—and worked to build—solidarity with one another. Russia, meanwhile, has redeployed soldiers that were active in Syria to Ukraine and Ukrainian forces have fought Russian forces in Syria, making the link between these two causes even clearer.

[2]

 Syrian aid workers have also volunteered in Ukraine, where they have drawn on their experiences dealing with Russia in their home country.

[3]

 Syrians took to the streets to declare their support for the Ukrainian resistance even before 2022,

[4]

 revealing an understanding that these two countries are now linked. Furthermore, the Assad regime is among the few governments to have recognized Russian-annexed Ukrainian territories as Russian,

[5]

 and Iranian weapons are being used in Russia’s ongoing campaign against Ukraine.

[6]


 Despite that, most Ukrainians remain seemingly uneducated about the Syrian struggle against the axis of Assad, Russia, and Iran beyond the knowledge of this mutual enemy. Furthermore, the difference in how Europe has received Ukrainian refugees versus how it has received Syrian refugees has led many to believe, understandably so, that the Ukrainian cause is valued in Europe while the Syrian one is not. This was worsened by racist European media coverage of Syrian refugees, especially when compared to coverage of Ukrainian refugees.

[7]

 In this chapter, I will explore how Ukrainians’ experience with Russian imperialism can serve as a bridge to other anti-imperialist struggles, and how arguments in favor of multipolarity fail to take into account similarities between authoritarian forces that nominally oppose one another—in other words, actually existing multipolarity. Instead, the experience of struggles on the peripheries suggests that, as with Ukrainians and Syrians, bond-building between victims of imperialism can help pave the way for truly anti-imperialist politics.


“Our Wounds Are Bridges”


 In 2022, I moderated a four-way panel featuring two Ukrainians and two Syrians as part of the “Post-Extractive Futures” series organized by War on Want, Tipping Point UK, JunteGente, and The Fire These Times.

[8]

 On the Ukrainian side were Yuliya Yurchenko, a senior lecturer and researcher in political economy at the University of Greenwich and the author of

Ukraine and the Empire of Capital

, and Taras Bilous, a historian, activist with the Social Movement organization, and editor for

Commons: Journal of Social Criticism

, covering war and nationalism. Bilous was also fighting on the front lines at the time of the conversation. On the Syrian side were Yassin al-Haj Saleh—a writer and former political prisoner, as well as the husband of Samira al-Khalil, a famed feminist activist who was abducted by the armed Islamist group Jaysh Al-Islam in Douma in December 2013—and Wafa Mustafa, an activist and detention survivor whose father was forcibly disappeared by the Assad regime in 2013. The conversation was recorded on YouTube

[9]

, and a transcription has been made available by Antidote Zine Collective.

[10]


 The title of the roundtable set the tone for the topic: “Our Wounds Are Bridges: The Threads that Bind Us from Syria to Ukraine.” The intention of the organizers, as stated in the announcement, was to provide “a space for mutual learning and solidarity-weaving amongst activists dreaming, enacting and mobilising toward …

title: Dominic Black - Rupturism and Popular Internationalism
content:
Author

: Dominic Black

Title

: Rupturism and Popular Internationalism

Subtitle

: An Open Letter of Political Divorce and Disassociation

Date

: September 6

th

, 2026

Source

: https://scissortailrising.substack.com/p/rupturism-and-popular-internationalism


 


Drafted by: Dominic Black


Adopted by: NLH, Anark, The Peaceful Revolutionary, Scissortail Anarchist Organization, Direct Action Distro, South Florida Anarchist Black Cross, Scissortail Anarchist Black Cross, FAFO Collective, El Monte


To Whom It May Concern


 There comes a point where disagreement and infighting cease to describe what is happening within the left.


 For more than a century, libertarian and authoritarian socialists have continued to speak as though we belonged to a single political family. We’ve inherited the language of a common Left, shared demonstrations, shared enemies, shared histories of labor struggle and antifascism, and, when circumstances demanded it, shared barricades. The depth of our problems have thus far been treated as a problem internal to that family: libertarian socialists distrust the state, authoritarian socialists insist upon transition; libertarian socialists demand autonomy, authoritarian socialists demand discipline; libertarian socialists warn against concentrated power, authoritarian socialists ask us to tolerate it until some later stage of history.


 This arrangement is impossible to maintain.


 What separates us isn’t principally a disagreement over which revolutionary strategy is more effective. Increasingly, we’re supporting different people, defending different institutions, recognizing different political subjects, and arriving at opposite sides of actual struggles with material, visceral consequences on the lives of others.


 Demanding freedom for prisoners of the Iranian state while simultaneously condemning American and Israeli imperialism should have been among the least controversial propositions imaginable for an internationalist Left. Nothing about opposition to prisons, executions, torture, foreign intervention, sanctions, or imperial war requires choosing one of those systems against another.


 Yet even this proved intolerable to a substantial campist tendency.


 People who insisted that Iranians could simultaneously oppose foreign imperialism and their own state were accused of assisting imperialism. Black radicals and abolitionists expressing solidarity with Iranian prisoners were subjected to demands that they withdraw their solidarity. Iranian voices describing their own repression were treated as politically inconvenient because acknowledging them disturbed a geopolitical narrative in which states, rather than the people governed by them, had become the principal actors of liberation.


 This occurred while anarchists across and connected to Southwest Asia and North Africa were already grieving another enormous loss. The autonomous project in Rojava. Imperfect, contradictory, never simply anarchist, yet among the closest contemporary revolutionary experiments to libertarian socialism. Rojava had been crushed beneath the new Syrian regime, US betrayal, and Turkish ethnic cleansing. For libertarian socialists who’ve spent years watching Kurdish, Arab, Assyrian, and other communities experiment with forms of communal autonomy, women’s liberation and confederal political organization under nearly impossible conditions, it was the destruction of a living revolutionary possibility.


 And almost immediately, we were again confronted by people calling themselves “anti-imperialists” who seemed unable to perceive liberation except through states.


 This is the rupture.


 The problem isn’t that anarchists and campists disagree over Iran, Syria, Palestine, Ukraine, China, Russia, or any other particular conflict. The problem is that we’re increasingly disagreeing over what anti-imperialism itself is, or who it’s for.


 For us, liberation belongs to the people. A government doesn’t become the embodiment of its population because it conflicts with Washington. A revolutionary party doesn’t become synonymous with the working class because it claims to represent it. A state does not acquire the right to imprison dissidents because another state wishes to overthrow it. A people do not cease to possess autonomy because their resistance complicates somebody else’s geopolitical strategy.


 No struggle against an empire can require us to abandon those living beneath another empire, state …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Eviction of 87-Year-Old Sparks Protest Encampment Over Spain’s Housing Crisis
content:
“We want to change the whole model of housing in Spain,” says Sabina Carrau of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal Martín in Madrid, after an investment fund bought her apartment building and more than tripled her rent, has become a symbol of Spain’s rising cost of living and sparked nationwide protests against corporate greed and wealth inequality. Over 600 protesters are now camped outside Madrid’s regional government headquarters demanding new tenant protections.

“What we have is a lot of furious people, enraged people, that are demanding from the government and from the public institutions that they give us give us some sort of solution,” says Sabina Carrau, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which is supporting the “Maricarmen decree” named after Abascal, set to be debated by Spain’s government this week.

Housing in Spain, as in much of the world, “is really connected to tourism, really connected to having and buying a house to make a speculation,” says socialist parliamentarian Tesh Sidi, who is calling instead for the guaranteed right to housing and “the right to have an affordable life.” Sidi, the only Sahrawi member of the Spanish parliament, also comments on Spain’s colonial relationship to Western Sahara and the state of Sahrawi rights and self-determination.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Today we’re broadcasting from London, tomorrow Copenhagen, and the rest of the week from Berlin. But we’re turning now to the Spanish capital of Madrid. A protest encampment over the cost of housing and housing instability has entered its third day as over 600 residents are now camped in front of the regional government headquarters at the Puerta del Sol plaza to demand new protections for tenants. Tens of thousands of people marched in the streets of Madrid Saturday. Demonstrations are also occurring across Spain.

Protests began Wednesday over the eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal Martín, referred to just as Maricarmen, who was forcibly removed from her home of more than 70 years after an investment fund bought her apartment building and more than tripled, or more, her rent. Police broke down the door of her home and removed Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, on a stretcher as hundreds of supporters gathered outside. She later released a video message to supporters from her hospital bed.

MARÍA DEL CARMEN ABASCAL MARTÍN: [translated] I have not been able to defend my home, but I have fought so others can learn to fight for theirs. My home has been my life, and now I have to leave it behind. But that doesn’t mean I’m not going to keep fighting.

AMY GOODMAN: Protesters, camped in tents with sleeping bags in the Puerta del Sol plaza, say they won’t leave unless meaningful government action is taken.

SARA BARROS: [translated] What we are demanding is that the rental market be regulated, because rents are unaffordable and people simply cannot afford them. There are abuses taking place that can leave vulnerable people out on the street, such as Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman with a disability who has no alternative housing after living in her home for 70 years.

LUCAS GARCIA: [translated] We are going to stay here until things change. There’s talk of a decree on Tuesday, and we will remain here until measures that we consider sufficient are adopted.

JORGE OTXOA: [translated] We are protesting so that we could claim and so the government listens to us, listens to a society that is tired of speculation, tired of corruption and tired of a system that sidelines the vast majority of the population. This is why we are here.

title: Kocaağa: Debt brake and social cuts deepened Germany’s crisis
content:
Muhlis Kocaağa, a member of Bremen's state parliament for Die Linke (The Left), discussed the reasons behind the rise of the far right in Germany, particularly in the eastern states, and Die Linke's role in opposing this trend.


Kocaağa said shrinking state budgets, the debt brake (Schuldenbremse) and cuts to social services had disrupted social stability. He also highlighted shortcomings in infrastructure and public services related to migration policies.


He said Germany was facing global geopolitical crises, rising energy costs, challenges arising from industrial transformation and a deepening housing crisis. Kocaağa stressed the urgent need to develop public and social policies to address these problems.


There has recently been a significant rise in the far right in Germany, particularly in eastern and North-Eastern Germany. How do you interpret this situation? Do you think the state is, in a sense, paving the way for it?


I assume you are referring to the state elections and the political situation in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, one of Germany's coastal states. There are two main reasons for this situation. My view differs somewhat from that of other politicians, and I have expressed it in political discussions as well.


The rise of the far right is generally attributed to the current government's social policies, particularly its tendency to restrict pensions, healthcare and social benefits. That certainly has an impact, but it is not the main determining factor. In my view, the fundamental reason is the existence of a deep-rooted, widespread right-wing tendency in Germany. Sometimes this tendency remains hidden, while at other times it emerges when the opportunity arises.


It reveals its true face whenever an opportunity for protest presents itself. This right-wing tendency has always existed in Germany, but it was less visible because the conditions were not favourable. Some attribute the current situation solely to opposition to government policies or to protest voters. Although protest voters certainly exist, we must not overlook the influence of the widespread right-wing tendency in Germany. Their existence does not change that underlying reality.


Some figures on the left, including those who were previously part of Die Linke but later formed the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), have suggested that they could break the firewall (Brandmauer) against Alternative for Germany (AfD) and form a government with it. How do you assess this position?


It is not always easy to predict how people's character will develop in politics. Even when these figures were part of Die Linke, they consistently adopted problematic positions in our discussions and were among those responsible for creating internal disputes within the party.


I consider their suggestion that they could break the firewall or cooperate with the AfD extremely dangerous for two reasons.


The first is their willingness to sacrifice everything for political power. It reflects an attitude of: "As long as I am in power, it doesn't matter what I have to sacrifice."


The second is their attempt to establish an opportunistic position for themselves in those regions. Ultimately, both approaches have the potential to harm society.


There has also been a noticeable increase in support for the left, particularly in Berlin. Die Linke lost votes in the early 2020s but has since seen its support rise. How do you explain this momentum?


The first reason is that the internal disputes and divisions within the party leadership have come to an end. The party's unity and solidarity have resonated positively with voters.


The second reason is that living conditions in Germany are becoming increasingly difficult. Die Linke is one of the parties offering the most concrete and consistent policies to make people's lives easier.


There is also a third factor we should not overlook: the rise of the right naturally strengthens its opposite. There is a significant group of voters who consciously support Die Linke in order to prevent the AfD from gaining votes.


Turning to budgetary constraints at state and municipal level, what is the situation regarding budget pressures, cuts to social services and infrastructure investment, particularly in cities such as Bremen and Bremerhaven?


The problem is not so much direct budget cuts as an enormous increase in spending requirements. For example, Bremerhaven's planned budget was around €700 million in 2023. It was initially …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec Liberal Sandrine Rioux prioritizes health care, housing, cost of living
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Quebec Liberal Party candidate Sandrine Rioux had to share with us.


Quebec Liberal Party candidate Sandrine Rioux said the reason she decided to run for office is simple: she wants to help people.


“My main goal is to help people, to be there, to be present, and to write good legislation at the National Assembly of Quebec,” said Rioux, speaking to Nunatsiaq News Tuesday from Chibougimou, where she was born and raised.


She’s among five candidates running in Ungava, the largest riding in the province geographically.


Her main priorities are improving access to health care, constructing more homes, addressing the cost of living and ensuring profits generated from resource development benefit communities.


Her party has a goal of building 100,000 homes per year in Quebec, she said, and wants to implement deadlines for housing authorities to encourage quicker development.


Each community, no matter how remote, should have a baseline 24-7 access to front-line health care services like doctors, nurses and pharmacists, she said. Telemedicine can fill gaps when specialists aren’t available.


At least five per cent of Quebec’s health budget should be dedicated to prevention, she said, and if elected, she wants to reduce Nunavik’s reliance on fly-in-fly-out health-care professionals.


Rioux has been involved with the Liberal party since 2019 and was president of its Ungava association.


She has a degree in business technology management from Université de Sherbrooke and a professional background in business analysis and marketing.


But she always held an interest in politics, she said, working for Élections Québec during the 2018 provincial election as an administrative assistant. It was one of her first jobs out of university and one that allowed her to visit each of Nunavik’s villages.


So far during the campaign, Rioux has visited Chapais, Chisasibi, Oujé-Bougoumou, Matagami, Mistissini, Radison, Waskaganish and Waswanipi. Travelling to Nunavik isn’t in the budget, but she said Kuujjuaq is first on her list if she gets elected.


“I really genuinely hope, if the people trust me, and invest in me, to be able to represent them at the National Assembly,” she said. “I want to make sure the lines of communication are always open.”
